title: Grade 2 daily reading
overview: A year of 180 authentic poems, tales, nature portraits, and short literary essays for adult read-aloud or shared reading. Each night allows 10–15 minutes for the text, rereading, and three or four conversations. Early selections emphasize sound and sequence; later ones ask for sustained memory, reasons for characters’ choices, careful observation, and more than one defensible interpretation. The year draws on twelve authors and twelve distinct works: Richards, Baldwin, Pyle, Baum, Farjeon’s London nursery rhymes (one series, recorded as separate source records only because each poem is supplied from the dated Punch issue or 1922 anthology that printed it), Cox, Blanchan, Bangs, the Grimms (Lucy Crane), Sandburg, Grahame, and Andersen (Mrs. H. B. Paull). The public-domain English editions retain historical language, with brief context where needed. Reading times and sequence are editorial teaching judgments, not measured levels or a claim that children can decode every text independently.

progression.focus: Listening for sound, sequence, and small surprises.
progression.rationale: Short complete poems invite repeated oral reading. Brief anecdotes ask listeners to explain one surprising action with a concrete detail; the first two-night scene asks them to remember a setting and follow a change in mood.

Nature portraits are read alongside animal fantasy. Children distinguish what a narrator observes from what a poet invents, while following more steps in an event and noticing the exact words that create sound or movement.

progression.focus: Fair exchanges, mistaken judgments, and practical help.
progression.rationale: Folktales and literary anecdotes offer different understandings of the same event. Shared discussion asks for reasons beyond a label such as good or bad and follows promises across linked scenes. Sandburg’s invented prairie tales add repetition, lists, and nonsense words that children can explain from the text.

progression.focus: Sustaining a story and noticing its construction.
progression.rationale: Consecutive passages, including two-night Sandburg stories, require a brief oral recap and attention to changes in goals, obstacles, and plans. Poetry continues to give shorter occasions for close rereading and comparison of literal with figurative meaning.

Readers compare what characters say with what their actions show, test a nature writer’s description against its stated observations, and explain jokes or surprising outcomes with more than one detail.

progression.focus: Taking a larger part in discussion.
progression.rationale: The child chooses an important phrase, supports a possible interpretation, and listens to an alternative. Longer fantasy scenes, complete verse narratives, and observational prose draw together memory, image, voice, and evidence; adults continue to support unfamiliar vocabulary.

days.title: Bird-Song
days.challenge: Hear how the repeated opening changes when the birds go to sleep.
days.focus: A day of nest-building becomes a song with four time settings.
days.context: Read once for the birds’ busy day, then let the child join the repeated first lines.

excerpt.locator:
Bird-Song; source blocks 262–265, beginning “Sweet! sweet! sweet! sweet!
Sing we in the morning,
Sending up to heaven's blue our happy ” and ending “
Singing, springing, with the breath of morning,
Waking up once more to all the wonder of the world.”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 70.

blocks.text:
Sweet! sweet! sweet! sweet!
Sing we in the morning,
Sending up to heaven's blue our happy waking song;
Daily, gayly, our tiny home adorning,
Working all so merrily the whole day long.

Soft, soft, soft, soft,
Sleep we through the still night;
Tiny head 'neath tiny wing comfortably curled,
Singing, springing, with the breath of morning,
Waking up once more to all the wonder of the world.

questions.prompt: What work have the birds partly finished at noon?
facilitatorNotes: They are building a nest from named materials. Trace morning work into the half-finished noon nest.
evidence: the moss and twigs are blended

questions.prompt: Why does “Sweet” turn into “Soft” in the last verse?
facilitatorNotes: The voices settle from daytime singing to nighttime sleep. A quieter reading can make the change audible.
evidence: Soft, soft, soft, soft

questions.prompt: Does the last verse simply end the birds’ day?
facilitatorNotes: It first gives rest, then looks ahead to waking again. The ending makes the day feel like a repeating circle.
evidence: Waking up once more to all the wonder of the world.

days.title: The Rain
days.challenge: Distinguish the household’s question from the rain’s answer.
days.focus: A talking rain shower answers a complaint with a surprising counterclaim.
days.context: Washing day meant hanging wet clothes to dry. The poem lets the rain speak for itself.

excerpt.locator:
The Rain; source blocks 55–56, beginning “The rain came down from the sky,
And we asked it the reason why
It would ne'er stay away
O” and ending “ng sound,
"Indeed, if I stayed
Till you called me," it said,
"I should not come all the year round!"”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 23.

blocks.text:
The rain came down from the sky,
And we asked it the reason why
It would ne'er stay away
On washing day,
To let our poor clothes get dry.

The rain came down on the ground,
With a clattering, pelting sound,
"Indeed, if I stayed
Till you called me," it said,
"I should not come all the year round!"

questions.prompt: Why do the people want the rain to wait?
facilitatorNotes: Their clothes cannot dry outside while it rains; their complaint comes from an ordinary household task.
evidence: To let our poor clothes get dry.

questions.prompt: How can you make “clattering, pelting” sound different from a gentle drizzle?
facilitatorNotes: Try the hard consonants and a quicker rhythm. The words suggest force and repeated striking, not only wetness.
evidence: With a clattering, pelting sound,

questions.prompt: What does the rain think would happen if it waited to be invited?
facilitatorNotes: It jokes that people would always find a reason to refuse rain. Consider whether the household and rain can both have a point.
evidence: I should not come all the year round!

days.focus: The listener knows more about farm animals than the searching speaker does.
days.context: The child speaker asks nearly everyone in the barnyard for an egg. “Dobbin” is a familiar name for a horse.

My grandmamma tol” and ending “g, but ten!

blocks.text:
Oh! how shall I get it, how shall I get it,—
A nice little new-laid egg?
My grandmamma told me to run to the barn-yard,
And see if just one I could beg.

"Moolly-cow, Moolly-cow, down in the meadow,
Have you any eggs, I pray?"
The Moolly-cow stares as if I were crazy,
And solemnly stalks away.

"Oh! Doggie, Doggie, perhaps you may have it,
That nice little egg for me."
But Doggie just wags his tail and capers,
And never an egg has he.

"Now, Dobbin, Dobbin, I'm sure you must have one,
Hid down in your manger there."
But Dobbin lays back his ears and whinnies,
With "Come and look, if you dare!"

"Piggywig, Piggywig, grunting and squealing,
Are you crying 'Fresh eggs for sale'?"
No! Piggy, you're very cold and unfeeling,
With that impudent quirk in your tail.

"You wise old Gobbler, you look so knowing,
I'm sure you can find me an egg.
You stupid old thing! just to say 'Gobble-gobble!'
And balance yourself on one leg."

Oh! how shall I get it, how shall I get it,—
That little white egg so small?
I've asked every animal here in the barn-yard,
And they won't give me any at all.

But after I'd hunted until I was tired,
I found—not one egg, but ten!
And you never could guess where they all were hidden,—
Right under our old speckled hen!

questions.prompt: Which request first tells you the searcher has the wrong idea about eggs?
facilitatorNotes: Asking the cow is an early clue; asking the dog or horse strengthens it. Let the child explain what those animals actually provide or do.
evidence: Moolly-cow, Moolly-cow, down in the meadow,

questions.prompt: Do the animals explain the mistake in words?
facilitatorNotes: They stare, wag, whinny, grunt, or gobble. These animal actions make a pattern of unanswered requests.
evidence: But Doggie just wags his tail and capers,

questions.prompt: Why is finding ten eggs funnier than finding the one requested?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker overlooked the obvious place and finds far more than expected. Readers may predict the hen well before the speaker does.
evidence: I found—not one egg, but ten!

days.title: Socrates and His House
days.challenge: Distinguish the neighbors’ idea of greatness from Socrates’ own.
days.focus: A tiny house gives a wise speaker an unexpected way to value friendship.
days.context: This is Baldwin’s literary retelling of an old anecdote, not a verified record of the conversation. Printed syllable breaks helped readers pronounce unfamiliar words.

excerpt.locator: Socrates and His House; source blocks 649–652, beginning “There once lived in Greece a very wise man whose name was Soc´ra-tes. Young men from all p” and ending “e; "but, small as the place is, I shall think myself happy if I can fill even it with true friends."”.

blocks.text: There once lived in Greece a very wise man whose name was Soc´ra-tes. Young men from all parts of the land went to him to learn wisdom from him; and he said so many pleasant things, and said them in so delightful a way, that no one ever grew tired of listening to him.
One summer he built himself a house, but it was so small that his neighbors wondered how he could be content with it.
"What is the reason," said they, "that you, who are so great a man, should build such a little box as this for your dwelling house?"
"Indeed, there may be little reason," said he; "but, small as the place is, I shall think myself happy if I can fill even it with true friends."

questions.prompt: Why are the neighbors surprised by the house?
facilitatorNotes: They expect a great man to need a great-sized house; they measure importance through size.
evidence: such a little box

questions.prompt: What does Socrates hope to fill the house with?
facilitatorNotes: He hopes for true friends, rather than possessions or an admiring crowd.
evidence: fill even it with true friends.

questions.prompt: Does his answer sound disappointed with the small house?
facilitatorNotes: It sounds content or gently challenging: even a small room full of real friends would make him happy. Different tones may be tried using his exact words.
evidence: I shall think myself happy

days.title: Orchard Street
days.challenge: Follow a changing list of visitors and hear how their names rhyme with fruit.
days.focus: A generous imaginary street built from rhyme, colour, and abundance.
days.context: An orchard grows fruit; here a London street name becomes a make-believe orchard. A pedlar sells goods, and a medlar and a quince are fruits. Reread the visitor-and-fruit pairs aloud.

excerpt.locator: Orchard Street; complete poem, opening “The fruit hangs ripe, the fruit hangs sweet,”, closing “Of the fruit that grows in my Orchard Street.”.

blocks.text:
The fruit hangs ripe, the fruit hangs sweet,
High and low in my Orchard Street,
Apples and pears, cherries and plums,
Something for everyone who comes.
If you're a Pedlar
I'll give you a medlar;
If you're a Prince
I'll give you a quince;
If you're a Queen,
A nectarine;
If you're the King
Take anything,
Apricots, mulberries, melons or red and white
Currants like rubies and pearls on a string!
Little girls each
Shall have a peach,
Boys shall have grapes that hang just out of reach—
Nothing's to pay, whatever you eat
Of the fruit that grows in my Orchard Street.

questions.prompt: What promise is made near the beginning, and which closing lines keep that promise?
facilitatorNotes: The promise is food for everyone; the ending makes all the fruit free. Ask the child to connect the broad promise with the absence of payment.
evidence: Something for everyone who comes.
Nothing's to pay, whatever you eat

questions.prompt: Why might the poet choose a medlar for a Pedlar and a quince for a Prince?
facilitatorNotes: Hear Pedlar/medlar and Prince/quince together. The matching sounds help invent the gifts; the poem does not argue that these are the visitors’ only possible favourites.
evidence: If you're a Pedlar
I'll give you a medlar;
If you're a Prince
I'll give you a quince;

questions.prompt: What do the rubies and pearls help you picture about the currants?
facilitatorNotes: Red and white currants become jewel-like beads along their stems. Children may notice shining colour, roundness, or a necklace-like arrangement if they connect it to the comparison.
evidence: Currants like rubies and pearls on a string!

days.title: What the Robins Sing in the Morning
days.challenge: Use sound words and repeated commands to hear the birds’ invitation.
days.focus: The morning appears as a gift waiting for the children.
days.context: “Shake the poppies from your eyes” is a playful way to say wake up, not an instruction about real flowers.

excerpt.locator:
What the Robins Sing in the Morning; source blocks 305–307, beginning “Wake! wake! children, wake!
Here we're singing for your sake,
Chirrup! chirrup! chirrup! c” and ending “ and dew,
All are waiting now for you.
Wake! wake! children, wake!
Here we're singing for your sake.”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 80.

blocks.text:
Wake! wake! children, wake!
Here we're singing for your sake,
Chirrup! chirrup! chirrup! chee!
Sweet a song as sweet can be.

Rise! rise! children, rise!
Shake the poppies from your eyes.
Sweet! sweet! chirrup! tweet!
Morning blossoms at your feet.

Song and sweetness, dawn and dew,
All are waiting now for you.
Wake! wake! children, wake!
Here we're singing for your sake.

questions.prompt: What do the robins ask the children to do twice?
facilitatorNotes: They call for waking and rising. Hear the repeated words as little bursts of birdsong.
evidence: Wake! wake! children, wake!

questions.prompt: Which line sounds most like a bird rather than an ordinary speaking person?
facilitatorNotes: The chirruping syllables imitate a bird call. Invite different performances without claiming there is one correct tune.
evidence: Chirrup! chirrup! chirrup! chee!

questions.prompt: What do the children gain by coming out in the morning?
facilitatorNotes: They gain song, blossoms, sweetness, dawn, and dew; the poem offers pleasures instead of scolding late sleepers.
evidence: Song and sweetness, dawn and dew,

days.title: Pot and Kettle
days.challenge: Notice that a speaker’s accusation may reveal something about the speaker.
days.focus: A reflection overturns the pot’s insulting judgment.
days.context: A shiny kettle can work like a mirror. These are imaginary talking kitchen utensils.
days.contentNote: The utensils’ blackness refers to soot on cookware. Their insults are part of the quarrel, not respectful ways to describe people.

excerpt.locator:
Pot and Kettle; source blocks 227–229, beginning “[To be read to little boys and girls who quarrel with each other.]” and ending “y image you see.
For I am so clear, without blemish or blot,
That your blackness is mirrored in me."”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 62.

blocks.text: [To be read to little boys and girls who quarrel with each other.]

"Oho! Oho!" said the pot to the kettle,
"You're dirty and ugly and black!
Sure no one would think you were made of metal,
Except when you're given a crack."

"Not so! not so!" kettle said to the pot.
"'Tis your own dirty image you see.
For I am so clear, without blemish or blot,
That your blackness is mirrored in me."

questions.prompt: What does the pot say is wrong with the kettle?
facilitatorNotes: It calls the kettle dirty and ugly; those are insults rather than a careful investigation.
evidence: You're dirty and ugly and black!

questions.prompt: What explanation does the kettle give for what the pot sees?
facilitatorNotes: The kettle says the dark image belongs to the pot reflected in its polished surface.
evidence: your blackness is mirrored in me.

questions.prompt: How would checking the reflection change the quarrel?
facilitatorNotes: The pot could recognize its own image and reconsider the accusation. The verse leaves the response for us to imagine.
evidence: 'Tis your own dirty image you see.

days.title: Three Men of Gotham
days.challenge: Separate imagined sheep from the real meal in the final demonstration.
days.focus: A quarrel about nothing leads to an argument that wastes something real.
days.context: This is Baldwin’s literary retelling of an old anecdote, not a verified record of the conversation. Printed syllable breaks helped readers pronounce unfamiliar words.

excerpt.locator: Three Men of Gotham; source blocks 212–234, beginning “There is a town in England called Go-tham, and many merry stories are told of the queer pe” and ending “stand here and quarrel about nothing, have no more sense in your heads than I have meal in my sack!"”.

blocks.text: There is a town in England called Go-tham, and many merry stories are told of the queer people who used to live there.
One day two men of Go-tham met on a bridge. Hodge was coming from the market, and Peter was going to the market.
"Where are you going?" said Hodge.
"I am going to the market to buy sheep," said Peter.
"Buy sheep?" said Hodge. "And which way will you bring them home?"
"I shall bring them over this bridge," said Peter.
"No, you shall not," said Hodge.
"Yes, but I will," said Peter.
"You shall not," said Hodge.
"I will," said Peter.
Then they beat with their sticks on the ground as though there had been a hundred sheep between them.
"Take care!" cried Peter. "Look out that my sheep don't jump on the bridge."
"I care not where they jump," said Hodge; "but they shall not go over it."
"But they shall," said Peter.
"Have a care," said Hodge; "for if you say too much, I will put my fingers in your mouth."
"Will you?" said Peter.

Just then another man of Gotham came from the market with a sack of meal on his horse. He heard his neigh-bors quar-rel-ing about sheep; but he could see no sheep between them, and so he stopped and spoke to them.
"Ah, you foolish fellows!" he cried. "It is strange that you will never learn wisdom.—Come here, Peter, and help me lay my sack on my shoul-der."
Peter did so, and the man carried his meal to the side of the bridge.
"Now look at me," he said, "and learn a lesson." And he opened the mouth of the sack, and poured all the meal into the river.
"Now, neighbors," he said, "can you tell how much meal is in my sack?"
"There is none at all!" cried Hodge and Peter together.
"You are right," said the man; "and you that stand here and quarrel about nothing, have no more sense in your heads than I have meal in my sack!"

questions.prompt: Where are the sheep while Peter and Hodge argue?
facilitatorNotes: Peter is only on his way to buy them; no sheep are on the bridge.
evidence: I am going to the market to buy sheep

questions.prompt: What is lost when the third man tries to teach a lesson?
facilitatorNotes: He pours his real sack of meal into the river. His demonstration costs food, unlike the imaginary sheep.
evidence: poured all the meal into the river.

questions.prompt: Is the third man as wise as he thinks he is?
facilitatorNotes: He notices the empty argument but wastes his own meal to prove it. Accept an argument for his insight or against his method, grounded in those actions.
evidence: learn a lesson.

days.title: Pepper & Salt: the storyteller’s preface
days.challenge: Understand a food comparison used to explain the purpose of stories.
days.focus: The author imagines humor as seasoning for everyday life.
days.context: Howard Pyle addresses his listeners while playing the part of a jester with a cap, bells, and bauble.

excerpt.locator: Pepper & Salt: the storyteller’s preface; source blocks 8–15, beginning “Here, my little man, you may hold my cap and bells,—and you, over there, may hold the baub” and ending “e you ready? Very well; then I will tell you a story, and it shall be about "The Skillful Huntsman."”. Full selected text also collated against Harper & Brothers 1886, scan leaves 10, 11.

blocks.text: Here, my little man, you may hold my cap and bells,—and you, over there, may hold the bauble! Now, then, I am ready to talk as a wise man should and am a giddy-pated jester no longer!
This is what I have to say:

One must have a little pinch of seasoning in this dull, heavy life of ours; one should never look to have all the troubles, the labors, and the cares, with never a whit of innocent jollity and mirth. Yes, one must smile now and then, if for nothing else than to lift the corners of the lips in laughter that are only too often dragged down in sorrow.

It is for this that I sit here now, telling you all manner of odd quips and jests until yon sober, wise man shakes his head and goes his way, thinking that I am even more of a shallow-witted knave than I really am. But, prut! Who cares for that? I am sure that I do not if you do not.

Yet listen! One must not look to have nothing but pepper and salt in this life of ours—no, indeed! At that rate we would be worse off than we are now. I only mean that it is a good and pleasant thing to have something to lend the more solid part a little savor now and then!

So, here I'll sit; and, perhaps, when you have been good children, and have learned your lessons or done your work, your mother will let you come and play a little while with me. I will always be ready and waiting for you here, and I will warrant your mother that I will do you no harm with anything that I may tell you. If I can only make you laugh and be merry for a little while, then my work will be well done, and I will be glad in the doing of it.
And now give me my cap and bells again, for my wits are growing cold without them; and you will be pleased to reach me my bauble once more, for I love to have him by me.
Will you be seated? And you, over there, seat the baby on the grass! Are you ready? Very well; then I will tell you a story, and it shall be about "The Skillful Huntsman."

questions.prompt: What kind of “seasoning” does the speaker offer?
facilitatorNotes: The seasoning is laughter, stories, and innocent fun, not literal pepper poured into the book.
evidence: a little pinch of seasoning

questions.prompt: Why does he also say life should not contain only pepper and salt?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines pleasure adding savor to ordinary duties; seasoning alone is not a meal. Children may discuss what else a day contains.
evidence: nothing but pepper and salt

questions.prompt: How do the cap and bells make the ending feel like the beginning of a performance?
facilitatorNotes: He takes back his jester’s equipment and seats the audience before starting a tale. It makes readers guests at a storytelling session.
evidence: give me my cap and bells again

days.title: Petticoat Lane
days.challenge: Hold several clothing descriptions in mind and distinguish the speaker’s favourite.
days.focus: A catalogue of colours and textures narrows to one personal choice.
days.context: A petticoat is a skirt worn beneath other clothing. Linsey-woolsey is cloth made from linen and wool; a nosegay is a small bunch of flowers. The poem imagines the street name as laundry hanging outside.

excerpt.locator: Petticoat Lane; complete poem, opening “Up the Lane and down the Lane and all round about”, closing “And one is sprigged with lavender, and that's the one for me.”.

blocks.text:
Up the Lane and down the Lane and all round about
The Petticoats on washing-day are all hanging out;
Some are made of linsey-woolsey, some are made of silk,
Some of them are green as grass and some are white as milk;
Frilled and flounced and quilted ones in Petticoat Lane,
Some are worked in coloured nosegays, some of them are plain,
Some are striped with red and blue as gaudy as can be,
And one is sprigged with lavender, and that's the one for me.

questions.prompt: Which two everyday things help you imagine the green and white petticoats?
facilitatorNotes: Grass supplies the green and milk the white. Invite the child to explain why these familiar things make the colours easy to picture.
evidence: Some of them are green as grass and some are white as milk;

questions.prompt: Are all the petticoats decorated the same way? Find two different kinds.
facilitatorNotes: The poem contrasts flower patterns and plain cloth, or stripes and lavender sprigs. Accept another pair accurately drawn from the poem.
evidence: Some are worked in coloured nosegays, some of them are plain,
Some are striped with red and blue as gaudy as can be,

questions.prompt: When do we learn which petticoat the speaker wants? How does that change the list?
facilitatorNotes: The last line chooses the lavender pattern. Earlier the speaker surveys many kinds; the ending turns the public scene into a personal preference.
evidence: And one is sprigged with lavender, and that's the one for me.

days.title: The First Tooth
days.challenge: Follow a comparison that changes tears into an ocean and a tooth into a pearl.
days.focus: An affectionate speaker gives a painful small event an imaginative happy ending.
days.context: A grown-up addresses a teething baby. The huge ocean of tears is playful exaggeration.

excerpt.locator:
The First Tooth; source blocks 33–38, beginning “My own little beautiful Baby,
You're weeping most bitterly, dear!
There'd soon be a lake, ” and ending “ life's happy years,
You'll show us the radiant pearl-drop
That you brought from the ocean of tears.”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 19.

blocks.text:
My own little beautiful Baby,
You're weeping most bitterly, dear!
There'd soon be a lake, if we treasured
Each sweet little silvery tear.

A lake? Nay! an ocean of sorrow
Would murmur and sigh at your feet,
And you would be drowned in your tear-drops,
My own little Baby sweet.

But, darling, as in the wide ocean
The divers plunge boldly down,
And bring up the radiant pearl-drops
To set in some royal crown,

E'en so from the sea of your sorrow,
This dolorous "fountain of youth,"
Will come, ere a week be over,
A little wee pearly tooth.

And then the tears will all vanish,
Dried up by the sunshine of smiles;
And we'll have back our own little Alice,
With her merriest frolics and wiles.

And whenever you laugh, my Baby,
Through all your life's happy years,
You'll show us the radiant pearl-drop
That you brought from the ocean of tears.

questions.prompt: Is there really enough crying to make an ocean? What does the exaggeration show?
facilitatorNotes: No literal ocean is meant; it enlarges how miserable the baby seems and how closely the speaker attends to her.
evidence: an ocean of sorrow

questions.prompt: Why is a pearl a good comparison for the new tooth?
facilitatorNotes: Both are small, pale, shiny treasures. In the poem both also emerge from a watery place.
evidence: A little wee pearly tooth.

questions.prompt: How does the final verse turn the baby’s future laughter into a reminder?
facilitatorNotes: Every smile showing the tooth recalls the earlier tears. The same object connects difficulty and pleasure.
evidence: That you brought from the ocean of tears.

days.title: Little Sunbeam
days.challenge: Separate the sunbeam’s mistaken explanation from what a reader can infer.
days.focus: Sunlight becomes a visitor astonished by a waking baby’s eyes.
days.context: The sunbeam is imagined as a little character. Read its visit through the garden and into a bedroom.

excerpt.locator:
Little Sunbeam; source blocks 124–130, beginning “Little yellow Sunbeam,
Waking up one day,
Down into the garden
Took her shining way;
Merri” and ending “Father, you must vanish!
Run and hide your head!
There's a brighter sun than you
In the baby's bed."”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 37, 38.

blocks.text:
Little yellow Sunbeam,
Waking up one day,
Down into the garden
Took her shining way;
Merrily went dancing
Down the morning air,
Shaking out the sparkles
From her golden hair.

Little yellow Sunbeam
Twinkled all about,
Down among the green leaves
Flitting in and out.
Waking up the daisies
From their morning doze,
Ringing up the lily-bells,
Knocking up the rose.

Little yellow Sunbeam,
Climbing up the wall,
On the baby's window
Happened for to fall.
In the little chamber
As she took a peep,
There she saw the Lovely One
Lying fast asleep.

Little yellow Sunbeam
Tripped into the room,
Sweeping out the darkness
With her golden broom.
All the little shadows,
Glimmering and gray,
Gathered up their dusky skirts,
Softly slid away.

Little yellow Sunbeam,
Flitting to the bed,
Merrily went dancing
Round the baby's head.
Suddenly there flashed out,
To her great surprise,
Other little sunbeams
From the baby's eyes.

Little yellow Sunbeam
Said, "How can this be?
Whence these little sparklers
So unlike to me?
Scarce I think they can be
Sunbeams real and true,
For we all are yellow;
These are lovely blue."

Little yellow Sunbeam
Flew back to the sky.
Running to her father,
She began to cry:
"Father, you must vanish!
Run and hide your head!
There's a brighter sun than you
In the baby's bed."

questions.prompt: How does the sunbeam get the sleepy flowers’ attention?
facilitatorNotes: It wakes daisies, rings lily-bells, and knocks up the rose. These house-visitor actions make the garden seem inhabited.
evidence: Ringing up the lily-bells,

questions.prompt: What really causes the “other little sunbeams” to appear?
facilitatorNotes: The baby opens bright eyes. The child can point out that the sunbeam interprets reflected light as rival sunbeams.
evidence: From the baby's eyes.

questions.prompt: Why does the sunbeam tell its father to hide?
facilitatorNotes: It believes the baby is a brighter sun. This is an affectionate exaggeration, not a claim about astronomy.
evidence: There's a brighter sun than you

days.title: Cornelia's Jewels
days.challenge: Recognize that the same word can name objects and express someone’s value.
days.focus: The glittering gems prepare a surprising second meaning of jewels.
days.context: This is Baldwin’s literary retelling of an old anecdote, not a verified record of the conversation. Printed syllable breaks helped readers pronounce unfamiliar words.

excerpt.locator: Cornelia's Jewels; source blocks 489–504, beginning “It was a bright morning in the old city of Rome many hundred years ago. In a vine-covered ” and ending “ought of this scene in the garden. And the world still likes to hear the story of Cornelia's jewels.”.

blocks.text: It was a bright morning in the old city of Rome many hundred years ago. In a vine-covered summer-house in a beautiful garden, two boys were standing. They were looking at their mother and her friend, who were walking among the flowers and trees.
"Did you ever see so handsome a lady as our mother's friend?" asked the younger boy, holding his tall brother's hand. "She looks like a queen."
"Yet she is not so beautiful as our mother," said the elder boy. "She has a fine dress, it is true; but her face is not noble and kind. It is our mother who is like a queen."
"That is true," said the other. "There is no woman in Rome so much like a queen as our own dear mother."

Soon Cor-ne´li-a, their mother, came down the walk to speak with them. She was simply dressed in a plain white robe. Her arms and feet were bare, as was the custom in those days; and no rings nor chains glit-tered about her hands and neck. For her only crown, long braids of soft brown hair were coiled about her head; and a tender smile lit up her noble face as she looked into her sons' proud eyes.
"Boys," she said, "I have something to tell you."
They bowed before her, as Roman lads were taught to do, and said, "What is it, mother?"
"You are to dine with us to-day, here in the garden; and then our friend is going to show us that wonderful casket of jewels of which you have heard so much."

The brothers looked shyly at their mother's friend. Was it possible that she had still other rings besides those on her fingers? Could she have other gems besides those which sparkled in the chains about her neck?

When the simple out-door meal was over, a servant brought the casket from the house. The lady opened it. Ah, how those jewels dazzled the eyes of the wondering boys! There were ropes of pearls, white as milk, and smooth as satin; heaps of shining rubies, red as the glowing coals; sap-phires as blue as the sky that summer day; and di-a-monds that flashed and sparkled like the sunlight.
The brothers looked long at the gems.
"Ah!" whis-pered the younger; "if our mother could only have such beautiful things!"
At last, how-ever, the casket was closed and carried care-ful-ly away.
"Is it true, Cor-ne-li-a, that you have no jewels?" asked her friend. "Is it true, as I have heard it whis-pered, that you are poor?"
"No, I am not poor," answered Cornelia, and as she spoke she drew her two boys to her side; "for here are my jewels. They are worth more than all your gems."

I am sure that the boys never forgot their mother's pride and love and care; and in after years, when they had become great men in Rome, they often thought of this scene in the garden. And the world still likes to hear the story of Cornelia's jewels.

questions.prompt: What do the boys notice about the visitor that differs from their mother?
facilitatorNotes: The visitor has rich clothes and jewelry; Cornelia wears a plain robe and no chains. Her kindness is a different kind of beauty.
evidence: no rings nor chains glit-tered about her hands and neck.

questions.prompt: Which comparisons help us picture the jewels in the box?
facilitatorNotes: Choose milk-white pearls, coal-red rubies, sky-blue sapphires, or sunlight-like diamonds and explain the color or brightness.
evidence: pearls, white as milk, and smooth as satin;

questions.prompt: Why does Cornelia pull her boys beside her before answering?
facilitatorNotes: The action identifies her children as her jewels. Her wealth is her love and pride in them, not a hidden necklace.
evidence: for here are my jewels.

days.title: Doctor Goldsmith
days.challenge: Use the household details to reconsider what kind of help is needed.
days.focus: A medicine box hides a practical act of generosity.
days.context: This is Baldwin’s literary retelling of an old anecdote, not a verified record of the conversation. Printed syllable breaks helped readers pronounce unfamiliar words.

excerpt.locator: Doctor Goldsmith; source blocks 688–701, beginning “There was once a kind man whose name was Oliver Gold-smith. He wrote many de-light-ful boo” and ending “Goldsmith had given them all the ready money that he had.”.

blocks.text: There was once a kind man whose name was Oliver Gold-smith. He wrote many de-light-ful books, some of which you will read when you are older.
He had a gentle heart. He was always ready to help others and to share with them anything that he had. He gave away so much to the poor that he was always poor himself.
He was some-times called Doctor Goldsmith; for he had studied to be a phy-si-cian.
One day a poor woman asked Doctor Goldsmith to go and see her husband, who was sick and could not eat.
Goldsmith did so. He found that the family was in great need. The man had not had work for a long time. He was not sick, but in distress; and, as for eating, there was no food in the house.
"Call at my room this evening," said Goldsmith to the woman, "and I will give you some med-i-cine for your husband."
In the evening the woman called. Goldsmith gave her a little paper box that was very heavy.
"Here is the med-i-cine," he said. "Use it faith-ful-ly, and I think it will do your husband a great deal of good. But don't open the box until you reach home."
"What are the di-rec-tions for taking it?" asked the woman.
"You will find them inside of the box," he answered.
When the woman reached her home, she sat down by her husband's side, and they opened the box; What do you think they found in it?
It was full of pieces of money. And on the top were the di-rec-tions:—
"TO BE TAKEN AS OFTEN AS NE-CES-SI-TY REQUIRES."
Goldsmith had given them all the ready money that he had.

questions.prompt: What does Goldsmith discover that changes his understanding of the illness?
facilitatorNotes: The family has no food because the man has been out of work. Do not generalize this story into medical advice.
evidence: there was no food in the house.

questions.prompt: Which detail hints that the box may contain something unexpected?
facilitatorNotes: Its heaviness makes a clue before the money is revealed. Children may also notice the instruction to open it at home.
evidence: a little paper box that was very heavy.

questions.prompt: Why call the money “medicine” in this story?
facilitatorNotes: It lets the family buy what they need. The word turns practical help into a kind of cure within the anecdote.
evidence: full of pieces of money.

days.title: Swiss Cottage
days.challenge: Follow repeated singing through eating, drinking, and asking for more.
days.focus: Repetition turns an ordinary meal into a noisy comic performance.
days.context: A jodeller is a yodeller, a singer who changes between high and low notes. Pottage is a thick soup or stew. Read once to follow the meal and again with a playful repeated rhythm.

excerpt.locator: Swiss Cottage; complete poem, opening “I heard a Jodeller”, closing “And jodelled for more!”.

blocks.text: I heard a Jodeller
In a Swiss cottage
Eating a crust
And a bowlful of pottage.
He jodelled and jodelled
'Twixt every bite;
He jodelled until
Not a crumb was in sight.
He jodelled and jodelled
'Twixt every sup;
He jodelled until
He had drunk it all up.
He put down his bowl
And he came to the door,
And jodelled and jodelled
And jodelled for more!

questions.prompt: What does the singer finish first, and what does he finish next?
facilitatorNotes: The crust disappears first; then he drinks the bowlful. Link “crumb” to the food and “sup” to a drink.
evidence: Not a crumb was in sight.
He had drunk it all up.

questions.prompt: What keeps interrupting every bite and every sip? Which repeated words let you hear it?
facilitatorNotes: He yodels between bites and drinks. The repeated “jodelled and jodelled” lets the listener imagine singing that hardly stops.
evidence: He jodelled and jodelled

questions.prompt: Does putting down the bowl end his performance? Explain the surprise at the door.
facilitatorNotes: No: he comes to the door and sings for more food. The final repetition makes the end of the meal the beginning of another request.
evidence: He put down his bowl
And jodelled for more!

days.title: The Postman
days.challenge: Hear the speaker’s change of attitude when the expected letter does not arrive.
days.focus: A repeated welcome becomes an unfair dismissal.
days.context: A postman delivers letters and bills. “Naught” means nothing; a “nag” is a horse.

excerpt.locator:
The Postman; source blocks 471–473, beginning “Hey! the little postman,
And his little dog.
Here he comes a-hopping
Like a little frog;
B” and ending “cat.
What is that he's saying?
"Naught for you to-day!"
Horrid little postman!
I wish you'd go away!”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 113.

blocks.text:
Hey! the little postman,
And his little dog.
Here he comes a-hopping
Like a little frog;
Bringing me a letter,
Bringing me a note,
In the little pocket
Of his little coat.

Hey! the little postman,
And his little bag,
Here he comes a-trotting
Like a little nag;
Bringing me a paper,
Bringing me a bill,
From the little grocer
On the little hill.

Hey! the little postman,
And his little hat,
Here he comes a-creeping
Like a little cat.
What is that he's saying?
"Naught for you to-day!"
Horrid little postman!
I wish you'd go away!

questions.prompt: Which three animal movements describe the postman’s approach?
facilitatorNotes: Hopping like a frog, trotting like a horse, and creeping like a cat turn deliveries into small performances.
evidence: Like a little frog;

questions.prompt: What news changes the speaker’s welcome?
facilitatorNotes: The postman has nothing for the speaker that day. It is not evidence that he has done his job badly.
evidence: Naught for you to-day!

questions.prompt: Is “Horrid little postman” a fair judgment?
facilitatorNotes: A child may recognize disappointment but distinguish it from wrongdoing by the messenger. Compare the earlier eager greetings.
evidence: Horrid little postman!

days.title: What Bobby Said
days.challenge: Infer an expectation that the speaker does not explain until halfway through.
days.focus: The egg’s unchanged inside exposes a child’s literal reading of its decoration.
days.context: Some families decorate eggs at Easter. Bobby expects the outside colors to continue inside.

excerpt.locator:
What Bobby Said; source blocks 591–597, beginning “I don't think it's right!
I don't think it's fair!
I don't like Easter
At all! so there!” and ending “I don't think it's right,
And I don't think it's fair,
And I don't like Easter
At all! so there!”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 142, 143.

blocks.text:
I don't think it's right!
I don't think it's fair!
I don't like Easter
At all! so there!

It's only because
I'm young, you see,
They think they can play
Their tricks upon me.

They brought me an egg,
And a beauty, too!
All golden yellow,
With stripes of blue.

They said 'twas a true egg,
A truly true!
And, of course, I supposed
It was so all through;

But when it was opened,
Just think what a shame!
'Twas just like the white ones,
Just 'zactly the same!

Part white and part yellow,
No bit of it blue,
And it tasted the same
As the other ones, too.

I don't think it's right,
And I don't think it's fair,
And I don't like Easter
At all! so there!

questions.prompt: Before the egg is opened, which colors make it seem special to Bobby?
facilitatorNotes: He sees golden yellow with blue stripes; keep the outside description separate from what is inside.
evidence:
All golden yellow,
With stripes of blue.

questions.prompt: What does Bobby take “a true egg” to mean?
facilitatorNotes: He appears to expect the decorated colors all the way through. The adults mean a real egg rather than a toy.
evidence: It was so all through;

questions.prompt: Why does the poem repeat the opening complaint at the end?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated outburst lets us hear the same words with new understanding of the small disappointment behind them.
evidence: I don't think it's fair!

days.title: The Miller of the Dee
days.challenge: Notice how a king can envy a worker who owns less.
days.focus: A song is corrected without destroying the singer’s happiness.
days.context: This is Baldwin’s literary retelling of an old anecdote, not a verified record of the conversation. Printed syllable breaks helped readers pronounce unfamiliar words.

excerpt.locator:
The Miller of the Dee; source blocks 280–291, beginning “Once upon a time there lived on the banks of the River Dee a miller, who was the hap-pi-es” and ending “"Oh, I'm as happy as happy can be,
For I live by the side of the River Dee!"”.

blocks.text: Once upon a time there lived on the banks of the River Dee a miller, who was the hap-pi-est man in England. He was always busy from morning till night, and he was always singing as merrily as any lark. He was so cheerful that he made everybody else cheerful; and people all over the land liked to talk about his pleasant ways. At last the king heard about him.
"I will go down and talk with this won-der-ful miller," he said. "Perhaps he can tell me how to be happy."
As soon as he stepped inside of the mill, he heard the miller singing:—
"You're wrong, my friend," said the king. "You're wrong as wrong can be. I envy you; and I would gladly change places with you, if I could only be as light-hearted as you are."
The miller smiled, and bowed to the king.
"I am sure I could not think of changing places with you, sir," he said.
"Now tell me," said the king, "what makes you so cheerful and glad here in your dusty mill, while I, who am king, am sad and in trouble every day."

The miller smiled again, and said, "I do not know why you are sad, but I can eas-i-ly tell why I am glad. I earn my own bread; I love my wife and my children; I love my friends, and they love me; and I owe not a penny to any man. Why should I not be happy? For here is the River Dee, and every day it turns my mill; and the mill grinds the corn that feeds my wife, my babes, and me."

"Say no more," said the king. "Stay where you are, and be happy still. But I envy you. Your dusty cap is worth more than my golden crown. Your mill does more for you than my kingdom can do for me. If there were more such men as you, what a good place this world would be! Good-by, my friend!"
The king turned about, and walked sadly away; and the miller went back to his work singing:—

"Oh, I'm as happy as happy can be,
For I live by the side of the River Dee!"

questions.prompt: Which part of the miller’s song does the king say is wrong?
facilitatorNotes: The king disputes “nobody envies me,” because he envies the miller’s happiness.
evidence: And nobody envies me.

questions.prompt: What does the river give the miller besides a pretty view?
facilitatorNotes: It turns the mill that grinds the corn and supports his household. Nature and work are connected.
evidence: every day it turns my mill;

questions.prompt: Why is the dusty cap worth more than a golden crown to the king?
facilitatorNotes: He values the contented life the cap represents. Discuss whether happiness, work, and loving relationships matter more here than rank.
evidence: Your dusty cap is worth more than my golden crown.

days.title: Bruce and the Spider
days.challenge: Connect two sequences of six failures without treating a story as proof.
days.focus: Careful attention to a spider changes the king’s willingness to try.
days.context: This is Baldwin’s literary retelling of an old anecdote, not a verified record of the conversation. Printed syllable breaks helped readers pronounce unfamiliar words.
days.contentNote: The background is a war, described without graphic injury. The spider episode is a traditional legend rather than established history.

excerpt.locator: Bruce and the Spider; source blocks 189–197, beginning “There was once a king of Scot-land whose name was Robert Bruce. He had need to be both bra” and ending “ever hurt a spider. The lesson which the little crea-ture had taught the king was never for-got-ten.”.

blocks.text: There was once a king of Scot-land whose name was Robert Bruce. He had need to be both brave and wise, for the times in which he lived were wild and rude. The King of England was at war with him, and had led a great army into Scotland to drive him out of the land.

Battle after battle had been fought. Six times had Bruce led his brave little army against his foes; and six times had his men been beaten, and driven into flight. At last his army was scat-tered, and he was forced to hide himself in the woods and in lonely places among the moun-tains.

One rainy day, Bruce lay on the ground under a rude shed, lis-ten-ing to the patter of the drops on the roof above him. He was tired and sick at heart, and ready to give up all hope. It seemed to him that there was no use for him to try to do anything more.

As he lay thinking, he saw a spider over his head, making ready to weave her web. He watched her as she toiled slowly and with great care. Six times she tried to throw her frail thread from one beam to another, and six times it fell short.
"Poor thing!" said Bruce: "you, too, know what it is to fail."

But the spider did not lose hope with the sixth failure. With still more care, she made ready to try for the seventh time. Bruce almost forgot his own troubles as he watched her swing herself out upon the slender line. Would she fail again? No! The thread was carried safely to the beam, and fas-tened there.
"I, too, will try a seventh time!" cried Bruce.

He arose and called his men together. He told them of his plans, and sent them out with mes-sa-ges of cheer to his dis-heart-ened people. Soon there was an army of brave Scotch-men around him. Another battle was fought, and the King of England was glad to go back into his own country.
I have heard it said, that, after that day, no one by the name of Bruce would ever hurt a spider. The lesson which the little crea-ture had taught the king was never for-got-ten.

questions.prompt: What number makes the spider’s efforts resemble Bruce’s?
facilitatorNotes: Both have failed six times; the repeated number links their situations.
evidence: Six times she tried to throw her frail thread

questions.prompt: Does the spider simply repeat without changing anything?
facilitatorNotes: The text says it tries with still more care. A useful reading includes attention and effort, not a guarantee that any seventh attempt works.
evidence: With still more care,

questions.prompt: What does Bruce do after watching the successful thread?
facilitatorNotes: He gathers people and makes plans. Watching inspires action rather than replacing the work.
evidence: He told them of his plans

days.title: King's Cross
days.challenge: Hear a place name become a sentence about an angry king, and contrast panic with calm advice.
days.focus: A repeated anxious question receives a small, practical answer.
days.context: King’s Cross is a London place name. In the poem “cross” also means angry. A sceptre is a ruler’s ceremonial staff and the Thames is a river. Read the final two lines more quietly than the frightened questions.

excerpt.locator: King's Cross; complete poem, opening “King's Cross!”, closing “For a minute or two.”.

blocks.text:
King's Cross!
What shall we do?
His purple robe
Is rent in two!
Out of his crown
He's torn the gems!
He's thrown his sceptre
Into the Thames!
The Court is shaking
In every shoe—
King's Cross!
What shall we do?
Leave him alone
For a minute or two.

questions.prompt: Which actions show that the king is more than a little annoyed?
facilitatorNotes: He tears his robe, pulls gems from his crown, and throws away his sceptre. Two of these details suffice; guide attention to actions rather than just repeating “cross.”
evidence:
His purple robe
Is rent in two!

He's thrown his sceptre
Into the Thames!

questions.prompt: What do the people around him keep asking, and what does that repetition suggest?
facilitatorNotes: They repeat “What shall we do?” and seem alarmed or unsure. The shaking court reinforces fear; other supported feelings such as helplessness are reasonable.
evidence: What shall we do?
The Court is shaking

questions.prompt: Why is the final advice a surprising answer to all that fuss?
facilitatorNotes: Instead of a grand rescue or punishment, it suggests briefly leaving him alone. The contrast between the damage and the tiny pause makes the ending funny.
evidence:
Leave him alone
For a minute or two.

days.title: Polly's Year
days.challenge: Compare a promise with a later report of what actually happened.
days.focus: Repeated sentence openings expose the distance between perfection and real life.
days.context: Uncle Ned asks Polly about the year on its first and last days. An adult can read the uncle and a child can read Polly with support.
days.contentNote: The poem repeats an old stereotype that boys make more noise than girls. Children of any gender can be noisy, quiet, careful, or careless.

excerpt.locator:
Polly's Year; source blocks 298–303, beginning “January 1.” and ending “n one of the boys.
In short, Uncle Ned, I very much fear
You must wait for my goodness another year.”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 79.

blocks.text: January 1.

Come sit on my knee and tell me here,
Polly, my dear, Polly, my dear,
What do you mean to do this year?

I mean to be good the whole year long,
And never do anything careless or wrong;
I mean to learn all my lessons right,
And do my sums, if I sit up all night.
I mean to keep all my frocks so clean,
Nurse never will say I'm "not fit to be seen."
I mean not to break even one of my toys,
And I never, oh! never will make any noise.
In short, Uncle Ned, as you'll very soon see,
The best little girl in the world I shall be.
December 31.

Come sit on my knee and let me hear,
Polly, my dear, Polly, my dear,
What you have done in the course of the year.

Oh dear! Uncle Ned, oh dear! and oh dear!
I'm afraid it has not been a very good year.
For somehow my sums would come out wrong,
And somehow my frocks wouldn't stay clean long.
And somehow I've often been dreadfully cross,
And somehow I broke my new rocking-horse.
And somehow Nurse says I have made such a noise,
I might just as well have been one of the boys.
In short, Uncle Ned, I very much fear
You must wait for my goodness another year.

questions.prompt: Which January promise would be especially hard to keep for a whole year?
facilitatorNotes: Any specific promise may be discussed: no noise, no broken toys, all clean clothes, or always correct sums. Explain why perfection is a very large promise.
evidence: never do anything careless or wrong;

questions.prompt: What word does Polly repeat in December instead of “I mean”?
facilitatorNotes: “Somehow” repeatedly makes the mishaps sound as if they happened on their own. Discuss whether she is puzzled, embarrassed, or avoiding responsibility.
evidence: And somehow I broke my new rocking-horse.

questions.prompt: What smaller promise could Polly make using one event she names?
facilitatorNotes: Accept a realistic plan tied to a detail, such as checking sums or treating the horse carefully. The text gives examples to revise rather than proof that Polly is hopeless.
evidence: You must wait for my goodness another year.

days.title: The Song of the Corn-Popper
days.challenge: Follow a process while listening to words that imitate its sounds.
days.focus: Hard kernels become imagined snow in a poem spoken by a cooking tool.
days.context: A corn-popper held kernels over a fire. Enjoy the sounds as reading; the historical cooking directions require adult handling of heat.

excerpt.locator:
The Song of the Corn-Popper; source blocks 584–589, beginning “Pip! pop! flippety flop!
Here am I, all ready to pop.
Girls and boys, the fire burns clear” and ending “s a treat for lad and lass.
Open your mouths now, all in a row;
Munch away! crunch away! here we go!”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 141, 142.

blocks.text:
Pip! pop! flippety flop!
Here am I, all ready to pop.
Girls and boys, the fire burns clear;
Gather about the chimney here.
Big ones, little ones, all in a row.
Hop away! pop away! here we go!

Pip! pop! flippety flop!
Into the bowl the kernels drop.
Sharp and hard and yellow and small;
Must say they don't look good at all.
But wait till they burst into warm white snow!
Hop away! pop away! here we go!

Pip! pop! flippety flop!
Don't fill me too full; shut down the top!
Rake out the coals in an even bed,
Topaz yellow and ruby red;
Shade your eyes from the fiery glow.
Hop away! pop away! here we go!

Pip! pop! flippety flop!
Shake me steadily; do not stop!
Backward and forward, not up and down;
Don't let me drop, or you'll burn it brown.
Never too high and never too low.
Hop away! pop away! here we go!

Pip! pop! flippety flop!
Now they are singing, and soon they'll hop.
Hi! the kernels begin to swell;
Ho! at last they are dancing well.
Puffs and fluffs of feathery snow,
Hop away! pop away! here we go!

questions.prompt: What are the kernels like before and after popping?
facilitatorNotes: Before they are hard, yellow, and small; afterward they are fluffy, white, and compared with snow.
evidence: Sharp and hard and yellow and small;

questions.prompt: Who is saying “Don’t fill me too full”?
facilitatorNotes: The corn-popper itself is the speaker. Its requests turn a household tool into the leader of the activity.
evidence: Don't fill me too full; shut down the top!

questions.prompt: How does the final “Munch away” change the repeated chorus?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated movement shifts from popping to eating, marking that the cooking is finished and everyone can share the treat.
evidence: Munch away! crunch away! here we go!

days.title: My Sunbeams
days.challenge: Work out when sunshine means light and when it means happiness.
days.focus: The children answer gloomy weather with action rather than waiting for the sky to change.
days.context: The Lovely is the baby. The older children are given playful nicknames as the speaker gathers them.

excerpt.locator:
My Sunbeams; source blocks 240–247, beginning “Oh, what shall we do for the Lovely
This rainy, rainy day?
Oh! how shall we make the baby ” and ending “sun, you may wander and roam;
And cry away, cry, you tiresome sky!
We've plenty of sunshine at home!”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 66, 67.

blocks.text:
Oh, what shall we do for the Lovely
This rainy, rainy day?
Oh! how shall we make the baby laugh,
When everything's dull and gray?

The sun has gone on a picnic,
The moon has gone to bed,
The tiresome sky does nothing but cry,
As if its best friend were dead.

Come hither, come hither, my Sunbeams!
Come one, and two, and three;
And now in a trice we'll have the room
As sunny as sunny can be.

Come, dimpling, dimpling Dumpling,
Come, Rosy, Posy Rose,
Come, little boy Billy a-toddling round
On little fat tottering toes.

Now twinkle, now twinkle, my Sunbeams!
Now twinkle and laugh and dance,
And brush me the gloom straight out of the room,
Nor leave it the ghost of a chance.

Aha! see the Lovely smile now!
Aha! see her jump and crow!
As round and round, with laugh and dance,
My three merry Sunbeams go.

And who cares now for the raindrops?
Who cares for the gloomy day,
When each little heart is doing its part
To make us all glad and gay?

questions.prompt: What problem does the speaker want to solve indoors?
facilitatorNotes: The aim is to make the baby laugh on a dull rainy day, not to stop the real rain.
evidence: how shall we make the baby laugh,

questions.prompt: Who are the three sunbeams invited into the room?
facilitatorNotes: They are children, named with affectionate nicknames. Their dancing and laughter brighten the mood.
evidence: Come, dimpling, dimpling Dumpling,

questions.prompt: How can the family have “sunshine at home” while the sky still cries?
facilitatorNotes: Sunshine now stands for the cheer they create together. The final weather images show the outdoor problem has not actually changed.
evidence: We've plenty of sunshine at home!

days.title: Alexander and Bucephalus
days.challenge: Use a small observed detail to explain a change in an animal’s behavior.
days.focus: The boy succeeds by noticing fear that the handlers overlook.
days.context: This is Baldwin’s literary retelling of an old anecdote, not a verified record of the conversation. Printed syllable breaks helped readers pronounce unfamiliar words.
days.contentNote: The story includes cruel handling of a frightened horse and fear that its rider could be hurt. It is a literary anecdote, not an activity to imitate.

excerpt.locator: Alexander and Bucephalus; source blocks 607–621, beginning “One day King Philip bought a fine horse called Bu-ceph´a-lus. He was a noble an-i-mal, and” and ending “through many countries and in many fierce battles, and more than once did he save his master's life.”.

blocks.text: One day King Philip bought a fine horse called Bu-ceph´a-lus. He was a noble an-i-mal, and the king paid a very high price for him. But he was wild and savage, and no man could mount him, or do anything at all with him.
They tried to whip him, but that only made him worse. At last the king bade his servants take him away.
"It is a pity to ruin so fine a horse as that," said Al-ex-an´der, the king's young son. "Those men do not know how to treat him."
"Perhaps you can do better than they," said his father scorn-ful-ly.
"I know," said Al-ex-an-der, "that, if you would only give me leave to try, I could manage this horse better than any one else."
"And if you fail to do so, what then?" asked Philip.
"I will pay you the price of the horse," said the lad.
While everybody was laughing, Alexander ran up to Bu-ceph-a-lus, and turned his head toward the sun. He had noticed that the horse was afraid of his own shadow.
He then spoke gently to the horse, and patted him with his hand. When he had qui-et-ed him a little, he made a quick spring, and leaped upon the horse's back.

Everybody expected to see the boy killed outright. But he kept his place, and let the horse run as fast as he would. By and by, when Bucephalus had become tired, Alexander reined him in, and rode back to the place where his father was standing.
All the men who were there shouted when they saw that the boy had proved himself to be the master of the horse.
He leaped to the ground, and his father ran and kissed him.
"My son," said the king, "Macedon is too small a place for you. You must seek a larger kingdom that will be worthy of you."

After that, Alexander and Bucephalus were the best of friends. They were said to be always together, for when one of them was seen, the other was sure to be not far away. But the horse would never allow any one to mount him but his master.

Alexander became the most famous king and warrior that was ever known; and for that reason he is always called Alexander the Great. Bucephalus carried him through many countries and in many fierce battles, and more than once did he save his master's life.

questions.prompt: What do the adults try that makes the horse’s behavior worse?
facilitatorNotes: Whipping increases the fear or struggle. The passage contrasts force with watching and calming.
evidence: They tried to whip him, but that only made him worse.

questions.prompt: Why does Alexander turn the horse toward the sun?
facilitatorNotes: He has seen that it fears its shadow; facing the sun moves the frightening shadow behind it.
evidence: the horse was afraid of his own shadow.

questions.prompt: What changes between the father’s first reply and his final greeting?
facilitatorNotes: He first speaks scornfully, then runs to kiss and praise his son. The boy’s observed success changes his judgment.
evidence: his father ran and kissed him.

days.title: Bishopsgate
days.challenge: Track two opposing groups on opposite sides of one gate.
days.focus: Mirrored phrases and opposing wishes create a noisy comic standstill.
days.context: “Without” here means outside and “within” means inside. Bishops are church leaders. The poem plays with the name of a London place by putting bishops on both sides of a gate.

excerpt.locator: Bishopsgate; complete poem, opening “Bishopsgate Without,”, closing “Inside, "Let me out."”.

blocks.text:
Bishopsgate Without,
Bishopsgate Within!
What a clamour at the gate,
O what a din!
Inside and outside
The Bishops bang and shout,
Outside crying, "Let me in!"
Inside, "Let me out."

questions.prompt: What does each group want the gate to let it do?
facilitatorNotes: The outside group wants to enter; the inside group wants to leave. Let the child point to two imagined sides while saying each request.
evidence: Outside crying, "Let me in!"
Inside, "Let me out."

questions.prompt: Which words make the scene sound noisy rather than peaceful?
facilitatorNotes: Clamour, din, bang, and shout all suggest noise. Try a quiet and a loud reading and compare which fits those words.
evidence: What a clamour at the gate,
The Bishops bang and shout,

questions.prompt: How do the last two lines echo each other while asking for opposite things?
facilitatorNotes: They repeat the location-plus-request pattern, but exchange outside/inside and in/out. The matching structure makes the disagreement easy to hear.
evidence: Outside crying, "Let me in!"
Inside, "Let me out."

days.title: King Canute on the Seashore
days.challenge: Recognize a test intended to expose flattering claims.
days.focus: The returning tide answers the courtiers more clearly than more praise could.
days.context: This is Baldwin’s literary retelling of an old anecdote, not a verified record of the conversation. Printed syllable breaks helped readers pronounce unfamiliar words.
days.contentNote: Baldwin opens with a broad unkind description of the Danes in an earlier war. That generalization is the nineteenth-century narrator’s language. The ending presents a Christian belief.

excerpt.locator: King Canute on the Seashore; source blocks 47–64, beginning “A hundred years or more after the time of Alfred the Great there was a king of England nam” and ending “ the ocean in the hollow of his hand. It is he whom you ought to praise and serve above all others."”.

blocks.text: A hundred years or more after the time of Alfred the Great there was a king of England named Ca-nuté. King Canute was a Dane; but the Danes were not so fierce and cruel then as they had been when they were at war with King Alfred.
The great men and of-fi-cers who were around King Canute were always praising him.
"You are the greatest man that ever lived," one would say.
Then an-oth-er would say, "O king! there can never be an-oth-er man so mighty as you."
And another would say, "Great Canute, there is nothing in the world that dares to dis-o-bey you."
The king was a man of sense, and he grew very tired of hearing such foolish speeches.

One day he was by the sea-shore, and his of-fi-cers were with him. They were praising him, as they were in the habit of doing. He thought that now he would teach them a lesson, and so he bade them set his chair on the beach close by the edge of the water.
"Am I the greatest man in the world?" he asked.
"O king!" they cried, "there is no one so mighty as you."
"Do all things obey me?" he asked.
"There is nothing that dares to dis-o-bey you, O king!" they said. "The world bows before you, and gives you honor."
"Will the sea obey me?" he asked; and he looked down at the little waves which were lapping the sand at his feet.
The foolish officers were puzzled, but they did not dare to say "No."
"Command it, O king! and it will obey," said one.
"Sea," cried Canute, "I command you to come no farther! Waves, stop your rolling, and do not dare to touch my feet!"

But the tide came in, just as it always did. The water rose higher and higher. It came up around the king's chair, and wet not only his feet, but also his robe. His officers stood about him, alarmed, and won-der-ing whether he was not mad.
Then Canute took off his crown, and threw it down upon the sand.

"I shall never wear it again," he said. "And do you, my men, learn a lesson from what you have seen. There is only one King who is all-powerful; and it is he who rules the sea, and holds the ocean in the hollow of his hand. It is he whom you ought to praise and serve above all others."

questions.prompt: Is Canute pleased when everyone keeps calling him mighty?
facilitatorNotes: He grows tired of their speeches and decides to teach them a lesson; he is not trying to prove the praise true.
evidence: grew very tired of hearing such foolish speeches.

questions.prompt: What visible result disproves the claim that everything obeys him?
facilitatorNotes: The tide wets his feet and robe despite his command. The actual result is stronger evidence than the courtiers’ promises.
evidence: wet not only his feet, but also his robe.

questions.prompt: Why does Canute take off his crown at the end?
facilitatorNotes: He rejects the idea that a human king has unlimited power. His final speech expresses the story’s Christian belief about God.
evidence: Then Canute took off his crown

days.title: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz: the author’s introduction
days.challenge: Hear an author’s claim about what kind of story he wants to tell.
days.focus: Baum sets a goal for pleasure and wonder before his fictional adventure begins.
days.context: This is Baum speaking about his book in April 1900, before the story begins. His broad claims about what all children enjoy are opinions.

excerpt.locator: Project Gutenberg 43936, 1900 George M. Hill text: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz: the author’s introduction; begins “Folk lore, legends, myths and fairy tales have followed childhood through the ages, for ev”; ends “L. Frank Baum. Chicago, April, 1900.”.

blocks.text: Folk lore, legends, myths and fairy tales have followed childhood through the ages, for every healthy youngster has a wholesome and instinctive love for stories fantastic, marvelous and manifestly unreal. The winged fairies of Grimm and Andersen have brought more happiness to childish hearts than all other human creations.

Yet the old-time fairy tale, having served for generations, may now be classed as "historical" in the children's library; for the time has come for a series of newer "wonder tales" in which the stereotyped genie, dwarf and fairy are eliminated, together with all the horrible and blood-curdling incident devised by their authors to point a fearsome moral to each tale. Modern education includes morality; therefore the modern child seeks only entertainment in its wonder-tales and gladly dispenses with all disagreeable incident.

Having this thought in mind, the story of "The Wonderful Wizard of Oz" was written solely to pleasure children of today. It aspires to being a modernized fairy tale, in which the wonderment and joy are retained and the heart-aches and nightmares are left out.
L. Frank Baum. Chicago, April, 1900.

questions.prompt: What does Baum say children love about fairy stories?
facilitatorNotes: He names the fantastic, marvelous, and unreal; ask for the distinction between enjoying an invented world and believing it is real.
evidence: stories fantastic, marvelous and manifestly unreal

questions.prompt: What feature of some older tales does he want to leave out?
facilitatorNotes: He objects to frightening incidents meant to enforce a lesson. His wording contrasts wonder with fear.
evidence: a fearsome moral

questions.prompt: What promise could you check while listening to Oz later?
facilitatorNotes: Readers can test whether the story brings wonder and joy, and whether it truly avoids all heartaches or nightmares. A promise is not proof of success.
evidence: the wonderment and joy are retained

days.title: The Cyclone, part 1: gray Kansas and the approaching storm
days.challenge: Notice a repeated color before tracking a sudden change from description to action.
days.focus: Dorothy’s laughter stands out against a dry, gray setting.
days.context: The novel opens at Dorothy’s Kansas home. She lives with Aunt Em, Uncle Henry, and her little dog Toto.
days.contentNote: Dorothy is separated from her aunt during a dangerous storm. This is fantasy, not guidance for tornado safety.

excerpt.locator: Project Gutenberg 43936, 1900 George M. Hill text: The Cyclone, part 1: gray Kansas and the approaching storm; begins “Dorothy lived in the midst of the great Kansas prairies, with Uncle Henry, who was a farme”; ends “nd the house shook so hard that she lost her footing and sat down suddenly upon the floor.”.

blocks.text: Dorothy lived in the midst of the great Kansas prairies, with Uncle Henry, who was a farmer, and Aunt Em, who was the farmer's wife. Their house was small, for the lumber to build it had to be carried by wagon many miles. There were four walls, a floor and a roof, which made one room; and this room contained a rusty looking cooking stove, a cupboard for the dishes, a table, three or four chairs, and the beds. Uncle Henry and Aunt Em had a big bed in one corner, and Dorothy a little bed in another corner. There was no garret at all, and no cellar—except a small hole, dug in the ground, called a cyclone cellar, where the family could go in case one of those great whirlwinds arose, mighty enough to crush any building in its path. It was reached by a trap-door in the middle of the floor, from which a ladder led down into the small, dark hole.

When Dorothy stood in the doorway and looked around, she could see nothing but the great gray prairie on every side. Not a tree nor a house broke the broad sweep of flat country that reached the edge of the sky in all directions. The sun had baked the plowed land into a gray mass, with little cracks running through it. Even the grass was not green, for the sun had burned the tops of the long blades until they were the same gray color to be seen everywhere. Once the house had been painted, but the sun blistered the paint and the rains washed it away, and now the house was as dull and gray as everything else.

When Aunt Em came there to live she was a young, pretty wife. The sun and wind had changed her, too. They had taken the sparkle from her eyes and left them a sober gray; they had taken the red from her cheeks and lips, and they were gray also. She was thin and gaunt, and never smiled, now. When Dorothy, who was an orphan, first came to her, Aunt Em had been so startled by the child's laughter that she would scream and press her hand upon her heart whenever Dorothy's merry voice reached her ears; and she still looked at the little girl with wonder that she could find anything to laugh at.

Uncle Henry never laughed. He worked hard from morning till night and did not know what joy was. He was gray also, from his long beard to his rough boots, and he looked stern and solemn, and rarely spoke.

It was Toto that made Dorothy laugh, and saved her from growing as gray as her other surroundings. Toto was not gray; he was a little black dog, with long, silky hair and small black eyes that twinkled merrily on either side of his funny, wee nose. Toto played all day long, and Dorothy played with him, and loved him dearly.

To-day, however, they were not playing. Uncle Henry sat upon the door-step and looked anxiously at the sky, which was even grayer than usual. Dorothy stood in the door with Toto in her arms, and looked at the sky too. Aunt Em was washing the dishes.

From the far north they heard a low wail of the wind, and Uncle Henry and Dorothy could see where the long grass bowed in waves before the coming storm. There now came a sharp whistling in the air from the south, and as they turned their eyes that way they saw ripples in the grass coming from that direction also.
Suddenly Uncle Henry stood up.
"There's a cyclone coming, Em," he called to his wife; "I'll go look after the stock." Then he ran toward the sheds where the cows and horses were kept.
Aunt Em dropped her work and came to the door. One glance told her of the danger close at hand.
"Quick, Dorothy!" she screamed; "run for the cellar!"

Toto jumped out of Dorothy's arms and hid under the bed, and the girl started to get him. Aunt Em, badly frightened, threw open the trap-door in the floor and climbed down the ladder into the small, dark hole. Dorothy caught Toto at last, and started to follow her aunt. When she was half way across the room there came a great shriek from the wind, and the house shook so hard that she lost her footing and sat down suddenly upon the floor.

questions.prompt: Why does “gray” appear so often in the description?
facilitatorNotes: It links the dry land, weathered house, and tired adults in one subdued mood. Toto and Dorothy’s laughter stand apart.
evidence: as dull and gray as everything else

questions.prompt: What makes Dorothy’s days different from Uncle Henry’s?
facilitatorNotes: Toto makes her laugh and plays with her; Henry works constantly and rarely speaks.
evidence: It was Toto that made Dorothy laugh

questions.prompt: Why is Dorothy still upstairs when the storm reaches the house?
facilitatorNotes: She goes to get Toto from under the bed instead of reaching the cellar with Aunt Em. Trace the steps without presenting this as safe storm behavior.
evidence: Toto jumped out of Dorothy's arms and hid under the bed

days.title: The Cyclone, part 2: a house in the air
days.challenge: Follow how fear changes over time even while the danger remains.
days.focus: Contrasting similes make a frightening journey strangely gentle.
days.context: The cyclone has struck before Dorothy and Toto could reach the cellar. Continue directly from the previous night.
days.contentNote: The storm and the floating house are fantasy. The passage’s explanation of cyclone air pressure is part of the old story, not a modern scientific account.

excerpt.locator: Project Gutenberg 43936, 1900 George M. Hill text: The Cyclone, part 2: a house in the air; begins “A strange thing then happened.”; ends “ the house and the wailing of the wind, Dorothy soon closed her eyes and fell fast asleep.”.

blocks.text: A strange thing then happened.
The house whirled around two or three times and rose slowly through the air. Dorothy felt as if she were going up in a balloon.

The north and south winds met where the house stood, and made it the exact center of the cyclone. In the middle of a cyclone the air is generally still, but the great pressure of the wind on every side of the house raised it up higher and higher, until it was at the very top of the cyclone; and there it remained and was carried miles and miles away as easily as you could carry a feather.

It was very dark, and the wind howled horribly around her, but Dorothy found she was riding quite easily. After the first few whirls around, and one other time when the house tipped badly, she felt as if she were being rocked gently, like a baby in a cradle.
Toto did not like it. He ran about the room, now here, now there, barking loudly; but Dorothy sat quite still on the floor and waited to see what would happen.

Once Toto got too near the open trap-door, and fell in; and at first the little girl thought she had lost him. But soon she saw one of his ears sticking up through the hole, for the strong pressure of the air was keeping him up so that he could not fall. She crept to the hole, caught Toto by the ear, and dragged him into the room again; afterward closing the trap-door so that no more accidents could happen.

Hour after hour passed away, and slowly Dorothy got over her fright; but she felt quite lonely, and the wind shrieked so loudly all about her that she nearly became deaf. At first she had wondered if she would be dashed to pieces when the house fell again; but as the hours passed and nothing terrible happened, she stopped worrying and resolved to wait calmly and see what the future would bring. At last she crawled over the swaying floor to her bed, and lay down upon it; and Toto followed and lay down beside her.
In spite of the swaying of the house and the wailing of the wind, Dorothy soon closed her eyes and fell fast asleep.

questions.prompt: Which comparison makes the rising house seem almost familiar?
facilitatorNotes: Dorothy first thinks of a balloon, then a cradle. These comparisons soften an impossible event without denying the wind’s noise.
evidence: as if she were going up in a balloon

questions.prompt: How does Dorothy keep Toto’s accident from happening a second time?
facilitatorNotes: After pulling him back she closes the trap door. Her practical action gives a small piece of control within the fantasy.
evidence: closing the trap-door so that no more accidents could happen

questions.prompt: Why can Dorothy finally fall asleep?
