facilitatorNotes: Hours pass without the feared crash; she becomes calmer and decides to wait. The rocking motion may help, but the text stresses her change from worrying.
evidence: she stopped worrying and resolved to wait calmly

days.title: Blackfriars
days.challenge: Keep track of a numbered catch-list and notice the object that breaks its pattern.
days.focus: A final unexpected catch overturns a rhythmic list.
days.context: Friars are members of a religious community; Blackfriars is also a London place name. A tiddler is a tiny fish, a winkle a small sea snail, and a dab a flatfish. This is a comic fishing rhyme, not a guide to river wildlife.

excerpt.locator: Blackfriars; complete poem, opening “Seven Black Friars sitting back to back”, closing “And the seventh one caught an old cart-wheel.”.

blocks.text:
Seven Black Friars sitting back to back
Fished from the bridge for a pike or a jack.
The first caught a tiddler, the second caught a crab,
The third caught a winkle, the fourth caught a dab,
The fifth caught a tadpole, the sixth caught an eel,
And the seventh one caught an old cart-wheel.

questions.prompt: What do the seven fishers hope to catch, and do their catches follow that plan?
facilitatorNotes: They hope for pike or jack, but the list gives a surprising variety instead, ending with a wheel. Ask for one mismatch from the list.
evidence: Fished from the bridge for a pike or a jack.

questions.prompt: What makes the seventh catch different from every earlier catch?
facilitatorNotes: It is an old cart-wheel, an object rather than a living creature. The built-up animal list makes this last catch especially surprising.
evidence: And the seventh one caught an old cart-wheel.

questions.prompt: How do “first,” “second,” and the later number words help you listen?
facilitatorNotes: They help keep the fishers and their catches in order and build expectation for the last one. Invite an ordered retelling using the actual catches, without requiring children to know every animal beforehand.
evidence: The first caught a tiddler, the second caught a crab,
The fifth caught a tadpole, the sixth caught an eel,

days.title: The Song of the Little Winds
days.challenge: Hear how one repeated sentence gathers three kinds of sleeper.
days.focus: The winds become gentle nighttime caregivers.
days.context: Listen once with eyes closed, then read the three opening pairs of lines together.

excerpt.locator:
The Song of the Little Winds; source blocks 83–85, beginning “The birdies may sleep, but the winds must wake
Early and late, for the birdies' sake.
Kiss” and ending “children's sake.
Singing so sweet in each little one's ear,
He thinks his mother's own song to hear.”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 29.

blocks.text:
The birdies may sleep, but the winds must wake
Early and late, for the birdies' sake.
Kissing them, fanning them, soft and sweet,
E'en till the dark and the dawning meet.

The flowers may sleep, but the winds must wake
Early and late, for the flowers' sake.
Rocking the buds on the rose-mother's breast,
Swinging the hyacinth-bells to rest.

The children may sleep, but the winds must wake
Early and late, for the children's sake.
Singing so sweet in each little one's ear,
He thinks his mother's own song to hear.

questions.prompt: Who may sleep while the winds stay awake?
facilitatorNotes: Birds, flowers, and children form the three groups; each receives a whole verse.
evidence: The children may sleep, but the winds must wake

questions.prompt: Which actions make the winds seem like a caring person?
facilitatorNotes: Kissing, fanning, rocking, and singing give the wind familiar soothing actions.
evidence: Rocking the buds on the rose-mother's breast,

questions.prompt: Why might the child mistake the wind’s sound for a mother’s song?
facilitatorNotes: Both sounds are imagined as soft and comforting. The ending brings the garden scene into a child’s own experience.
evidence: He thinks his mother's own song to hear.

days.title: Downy Woodpecker — a bird portrait (excerpt)
days.challenge: Connect a general description of friendliness with specific visits.
days.focus: A tiny drummer brings woodland activity close to people.
days.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897. A tattoo here means a repeated drumbeat. Listen for the places where this small bird appears.

excerpt.locator: Downy Woodpecker entry, narrative paragraphs beginning “He is very social with birds and men alike. In winter he attaches himself to strolling ban” and ending “ng on some resonant limb under our windows in the garden with a strength worthy of a larger drummer.”.

blocks.text: He is very social with birds and men alike. In winter he attaches himself to strolling bands of nuthatches and chickadees, and in summer is fond of making friendly visits among village folk, frequenting the shade trees of the streets and grapevines of back gardens. He has even been known to fearlessly peck at flies on window panes.

In contrast to his large brother woodpecker, who is seldom drawn from timber lands, the little downy member of the family brings the comfort of his cheery presence to country homes, beating his rolling tattoo in spring on some resonant limb under our windows in the garden with a strength worthy of a larger drummer.

questions.prompt: What two kinds of company does the downy woodpecker keep in this portrait?
facilitatorNotes: It travels with other birds in winter and visits places where people live in summer. Name nuthatches or chickadees and a village setting.
evidence: He is very social with birds and men alike.

questions.prompt: Which visit brings the bird especially close to a person looking out of a house?
facilitatorNotes: It pecks at flies on window panes. This concrete detail supports the author’s description of fearlessness.
evidence: He has even been known to fearlessly peck at flies on window panes.

questions.prompt: Why compare this little woodpecker with a larger drummer?
facilitatorNotes: Its powerful rolling sound seems unexpectedly large for its body. The comparison praises the sound’s strength, not the bird’s actual size.
evidence: with a strength worthy of a larger drummer.

days.title: The Brownies On Bicycles
days.challenge: Compare an observer’s easy description of riding with the later ride.
days.focus: Comic confidence meets wet paint and crowded steering.
days.context: Brownies are imaginary little sprites who act secretly at night. Wheelmen are bicyclists. These magical riders can handle impossible equipment; follow the poem’s comedy rather than treating it as riding instructions.

excerpt.locator: THE BROWNIES ON BICYCLES. Text blocks 1–10; opening “ONE evening Brownies, peeping down”; closing “An hour before the thrush awoke.”.

blocks.text:
ONE evening Brownies, peeping down
From bluffs that overlooked the town,
Saw wheelmen passing to and fro
Upon the boulevard below.
"It seems," said one, "an easy trick,
The wheel goes 'round so smooth and quick;
You simply sit and work your feet
And glide with grace along the street.
The pleasure would be fine indeed
If _we_ could thus in line proceed."

"Last night," another answer made,
"As by the river's bank I strayed,
Where here and there a building stands,
And town and country-side join hands,
Before me stood a massive wall
With engine-rooms and chimneys tall.

"Though built to keep intruders out,
With shutters thick and casings stout,
I noticed twenty ways or more,
By roof, by window, wall and door,
Where we, by exercising skill,
May travel in and out at will."

Another spoke, in nowise slow
To catch at pleasures as they go,
And said, "Why let another day
Come creeping in to drag away?
Let's active measures now employ
To seize at once the promised joy.
On bicycles quick let us ride,
While yet our wants may be supplied."

So when the town grew hushed and still,
The Brownies ventured down the hill.
And soon the band was drawing nigh
The building with the chimneys high.

When people lock their doors at night,
And double-bolt them left and right,
And think through patents, new and old,
To leave the burglars in the cold,
The cunning Brownies smile to see
The springing bolt and turning key;
For well they know if fancy leads
Their band to venture daring deeds,
The miser's gold, the merchant's ware
To them is open as the air.

Not long could door or windows stand
Fast locked before the Brownie band;
And soon the bicycles they sought
From every room and bench were brought.
The rogues ere long began to show
As many colors as the bow;
For paint and varnish lately spread
Besmeared them all from foot to head.
Some turned to jay-birds in a minute,
And some as quick might shame the linnet;
While more with crimson-tinted breast
Seemed fitted for the robin's nest.

But whether red or green or blue,
The work on hand was hurried through;
They took the wheels from blacksmith fires,
Though wanting bolts and even tires,
And rigged the parts with skill and speed
To answer well their pressing need.
And soon, enough were made complete
To give the greater part a seat,
And let the rest through cunning find
Some way of hanging on behind.
And then no spurt along the road,
Or 'round the yard their courage showed,
But twenty times a measured mile
They whirled away in single file,
Or bunched together in a crowd
If width of road or skill allowed.
At times, while rolling down the grade,
Collisions some confusion made,
For every member of the band,
At steering wished to try his hand;
Though some, perhaps, were not designed
For labor of that special kind.

But Brownies are the folk to bear
Misfortunes with unruffled air;
So on through rough and smooth they spun
Until the turning-point was won.
Then back they wheeled with every spoke,
An hour before the thrush awoke.

questions.prompt: How does the first Brownie make bicycle riding sound easy? Does the actual ride stay that simple?
facilitatorNotes: He reduces it to sitting and working feet; later collisions and competing steerers complicate that picture.
evidence: You simply sit and work your feet
Collisions some confusion made,

questions.prompt: Why do the Brownies suddenly resemble colourful birds?
facilitatorNotes: Wet paint and varnish colour their clothes and bodies; robin-like red breasts make the comparison particularly visible.
evidence: For paint and varnish lately spread
Seemed fitted for the robin's nest.

questions.prompt: What particular disagreement helps cause confusion on the road?
facilitatorNotes: Everyone wants to steer, although some are not suited to it. Distinguish too many commanders from a simple shortage of bicycles.
evidence: At steering wished to try his hand;

days.title: The Mouse
days.challenge: Listen for different ways a frightened speaker tries to persuade.
days.focus: The mouse turns an unwelcome visit into a plea for mercy.
days.context: The mouse addresses a woman as “Ma’am.” A rind is the outside of a piece of cheese.
days.contentNote: The mouse fears being killed and mentions a knife; no injury occurs.

excerpt.locator:
The Mouse; source blocks 396–401, beginning “I'm only a poor little mouse, Ma'am.
I live in the wall of your house, Ma'am.
With a fragm” and ending “am.
I'll slip through the crack,
And I'll never come back,
Oh! I'll never come back any more, Ma'am!”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 97, 98.

blocks.text:
I'm only a poor little mouse, Ma'am.
I live in the wall of your house, Ma'am.
With a fragment of cheese,
And a very few peas,
I was having a little carouse, Ma'am.

No mischief at all I intend, Ma'am.
I hope you will act as my friend, Ma'am.
If my life you should take,
Many hearts it would break,
And the mischief would be without end, Ma'am.

My wife lives in there, in the crack, Ma'am,
She's waiting for me to come back, Ma'am.
She hoped I might find
A bit of a rind,
For the children their dinner do lack, Ma'am.

'Tis hard living there in the wall, Ma'am,
For plaster and mortar will pall, Ma'am,
On the minds of the young,
And when specially hung—
Ry, upon their poor father they'll fall, Ma'am.

I never was given to strife, Ma'am,—
(Don't look at that terrible knife, Ma'am!)
The noise overhead
That disturbs you in bed,
'Tis the rats, I will venture my life, Ma'am.

In your eyes I see mercy, I'm sure, Ma'am.
Oh, there's no need to open the door, Ma'am.
I'll slip through the crack,
And I'll never come back,
Oh! I'll never come back any more, Ma'am!

questions.prompt: Why does the mouse describe a wife and hungry children?
facilitatorNotes: The family gives the listener a reason to care beyond the missing cheese. The mouse wants to appear responsible rather than troublesome.
evidence: For the children their dinner do lack, Ma'am.

questions.prompt: Who does the mouse blame for the nighttime noise? Can we be sure?
facilitatorNotes: It blames rats; we have only the mouse’s word, and it has a reason to avoid blame.
evidence: 'Tis the rats, I will venture my life, Ma'am.

questions.prompt: What does repeating “I’ll never come back” reveal?
facilitatorNotes: The repetition intensifies its fear and its promise. Try a confident and a hurried voice and decide which fits the escape.
evidence: Oh! I'll never come back any more, Ma'am!

days.title: Chickadee — a bird portrait (excerpt)
days.challenge: Compare a bird’s winter voice, feeding, and summer nesting.
days.focus: A cheerful winter companion also receives a practical defence.
days.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897. An entomologist studies insects. The author quotes old estimates and feeding practices; read these as part of the historical account. Adults can explain utilitarian as useful.
days.contentNote: Includes historical feeding advice and numerical estimates, presented as period nature writing rather than instructions or verified present-day measurements.

excerpt.locator: Chickadee entry, narrative paragraphs beginning “No "fair weather friend" is the jolly little chickadee. In the depth of the autumn equinoc” and ending “s the chickadee-dee-dee that Thoreau likens to "silver tinkling" as he heard it on a frosty morning.”.

blocks.text: No "fair weather friend" is the jolly little chickadee. In the depth of the autumn equinoctial storm it returns to the tops of the trees close by the house, where, through the sunshine, snow, and tempest of the entire winter, you may hear its cheery, irrepressible chickadee-dee-dee-dee or day-day-day as it swings around the dangling cones of the evergreens. It fairly overflows with good spirits, and is never more contagiously gay than in a snowstorm. So active, so friendly and cheering, what would the long northern winters be like without this lovable little neighbor?

It serves a more utilitarian purpose, however, than bracing faint-hearted spirits. "There is no bird that compares with it in destroying the female canker-worm moths and their eggs," writes a well-known entomologist. He calculates that as a chickadee destroys about 5,500 eggs in one day, it will eat 138,750 eggs in the twenty-five days it takes the canker-worm moth to crawl up the trees. The moral that it pays to attract chickadees about your home by feeding them in winter is obvious. Mrs. Mabel Osgood Wright, in her delightful and helpful book "Birdcraft," tells us how she makes a sort of a bird-hash of finely minced raw meat, waste canary-seed, buckwheat, and cracked oats, which she scatters in a sheltered spot for all the winter birds. The way this is consumed leaves no doubt of its popularity. A raw bone, hung from an evergreen limb, is equally appreciated.

Friendly as the chickadee is—and Dr. Abbott declares it the tamest bird we have—it prefers well-timbered districts, especially where there are red-bud trees, when it is time to nest. It is very often clever enough to leave the labor of hollowing out a nest in the tree-trunk to the woodpecker or nuthatch, whose old homes it readily appropriates; or, when these birds object, a knot-hole or a hollow fence-rail answers every purpose. Here, in the summer woods, when family cares beset it, a plaintive, minor whistle replaces the chickadee-dee-dee that Thoreau likens to "silver tinkling" as he heard it on a frosty morning.

questions.prompt: Why is “no fair weather friend” a good play on words for this chickadee?
facilitatorNotes: The bird remains through actual storms and cheers the observer in difficult weather, echoing a faithful friend.
evidence: through the sunshine, snow, and tempest of the entire winter

questions.prompt: After praising good spirits, what different reason does the author offer for valuing chickadees?
facilitatorNotes: They eat many moths and eggs. Separate the practical insect-eating reason from the delight of hearing the bird; the huge quoted numbers are historical estimates, not a counting task.
evidence: It serves a more utilitarian purpose, however, than bracing faint-hearted spirits.

questions.prompt: How can the chickadee obtain a home without doing all the hollowing itself?
facilitatorNotes: It uses an old woodpecker or nuthatch home, or a ready-made hole. That detail supports the playful description “clever enough.”
evidence: a knot-hole or a hollow fence-rail answers every purpose.

days.title: The Ambitious Chicken
days.challenge: Use early material details to understand an impossible character.
days.focus: Grand plans collide with the limits of a small decoration.
days.context: This is an imaginary talking Easter ornament, made of plaster, down, and beads. “Pate” means head.
days.contentNote: A toy chicken’s head breaks off. No real animal is injured.

excerpt.locator:
An Ambitious Chicken; source blocks 434–445, beginning “It was an Easter chicken
So blithesome and so gay;
He peeped from out his plaster shell
Al” and ending “ blue eyes,
And "Oh! Mamma!" she said:
"One piece has gone and popped itself
Into a chicken's head!"”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 105, 106.

blocks.text:
It was an Easter chicken
So blithesome and so gay;
He peeped from out his plaster shell
All on an Easter Day.

His wings were made of yellow down,
His eyes were made of beads;
He seemed, in very sooth, to have
All that a chicken needs.

He winked and blinked and peeped about,
And to himself he said,
"When first a chicken leaves the shell,
Of course he must be fed.

"And though I may be young in years,
And this my natal morn,
I'm quite, quite old enough to know
Where people keep the corn."

He winked and blinked and peeped about,
Till in a corner sly
He saw a heap of golden corn
Piled on a platter high.

"Now, this is well!" the chicken cried;
"Now, this is well, in sooth.
This corn shall nourish and sustain
My faint and tender youth.

"And I shall grow and grow apace,
And come to high estate,
With mighty feathers in my tail,
And combs upon my pate.

"To see my beauty and my grace
The feathered race will flock,
And all will bow them low before
The mighty Easter Cock."

As thus the chicken proudly spake,
And stooped to snatch the prize,
His head fell off, and rolled away
Before his very eyes!!!!

It rolled into the dish of corn,
A sad and sombre sight,
While still upon its plaster legs,
His body stood upright.

And little Mary, when she came
With shining "popper" bright,
To pop the corn, and make the balls
Which were her heart's delight,

Gazed at the dish with wide blue eyes,
And "Oh! Mamma!" she said:
"One piece has gone and popped itself
Into a chicken's head!"

questions.prompt: Which early clues show that this is a toy chicken?
facilitatorNotes: The shell is plaster and the eyes are beads; these details prepare the later breakage.
evidence: His eyes were made of beads;

questions.prompt: How far do the chicken’s plans go beyond having a meal?
facilitatorNotes: He expects to grow into a splendid ruler whom all other birds admire. His ambition expands through several verses.
evidence: The mighty Easter Cock.

questions.prompt: Why does Mary think corn has popped into a head?
facilitatorNotes: She arrives after the toy breaks, sees only its head among the kernels, and supplies her own mistaken explanation.
evidence: One piece has gone and popped itself

days.title: House Wren — a bird portrait (excerpt)
days.challenge: Extend a comparison across several verbs instead of stopping at one image.
days.focus: A song becomes a spring stream, then the portrait adds an unexpected temper.
days.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897. Eaves are the edges of a roof; a crevice is a narrow gap. This opening introduces a returning house wren and stops before the account of its eggs.

excerpt.locator: House Wren entry, narrative paragraphs beginning “Early some morning in April there will go off under your window that most delightful of al” and ending “ the house wren, its temper can put to flight even the English sparrow. Need description go further?”.

blocks.text: Early some morning in April there will go off under your window that most delightful of all alarm-clocks—the tiny, friendly house wren, just returned from a long visit south. Like some little mountain spring that, having been imprisoned by winter ice, now bubbles up in the spring sunshine, and goes rippling along over the pebbles, tumbling over itself in merry cascades, so this little wren's song bubbles, ripples, cascades in a miniature torrent of ecstasy.

Year after year these birds return to the same nesting places: a box set up against the house, a crevice in the barn, a niche under the eaves; but once home, always home to them. The nest is kept scrupulously clean; the house-cleaning, like the house-building and renovating, being accompanied by the cheeriest of songs, that makes the bird fairly tremble by its intensity. But however angelic the voice of the house wren, its temper can put to flight even the English sparrow. Need description go further?

questions.prompt: How can a bird be an alarm-clock without being a machine?
facilitatorNotes: Its early song wakes or alerts the listener beneath the window. The image locates both the sound and the time of day.
evidence: that most delightful of all alarm-clocks

questions.prompt: Which water actions help you hear the wren’s song?
facilitatorNotes: Bubbling, rippling and cascading suggest quick flowing notes. Reread that sentence slowly and invite an imagined sound pattern rather than a scientific imitation.
evidence: this little wren's song bubbles, ripples, cascades

questions.prompt: What surprise prevents the portrait from making the wren seem gentle in every way?
facilitatorNotes: Its beautiful voice contrasts with a temper fierce enough to drive off another bird. A lovely sound does not tell the whole story.
evidence: its temper can put to flight even the English sparrow.

days.title: The Brownies' Ride — Harnessing the mare (excerpt)
days.challenge: Keep separate the jobs needed before the cart can move.
days.focus: A small army of helpers prepares something much larger than themselves.
days.context: Brownies are imaginary little sprites who act secretly at night. The excerpt ends when the harnessed horse and cart are ready. A trace is a harness strap; the shafts are the cart’s long supporting poles.

excerpt.locator: THE BROWNIES' RIDE. Text blocks 1–7; opening “ONE night a cunning Brownie band”; closing “And horse and cart moved off as one.”.

blocks.text:
ONE night a cunning Brownie band
Was roaming through a farmer's land,
And while the rogues went prying 'round,
The farmer's mare at rest they found;
And peeping through the stable-door,
They saw the harness that she wore.
The sight was tempting to the eye,
For there the cart was standing nigh.

Now, Brownies seldom idle stand
When there's a chance for fun at hand.

So plans were laid without delay;
The mare was dragged from oats and hay,
The harness from the peg they drew,
And every one to action flew.
It was a sight one should behold
To see them working, young and old;
Two wrinkled elves, like leather browned,
Whose beards descended near the ground,
Along with youngsters did their best
With all the ardor of the rest.

While some prepared a rein or trace,
Another slid the bit in place;
More buckled bands with all their might,
Or drew the harness close and tight.

When every strap a buckle found,
And every part was safe and sound,
Then 'round the cart the Brownies flew,--
The hardest task was yet to do.
It often puzzles bearded men,
Though o'er and o'er performed again.

Some held the shafts to steer them straight,
More did their best to balance weight,
While others showed both strength and art
In backing Mag into the cart.
At length the heavy job was done,
And horse and cart moved off as one.

questions.prompt: What has one Brownie actually seen that makes him trust the mare’s strength?
facilitatorNotes: He remembers her carrying a ton of hay uphill without being whipped. This is observed evidence rather than merely calling her strong.
evidence: Until her load--a ton of hay--

questions.prompt: Which details show both old and young Brownies sharing the preparation?
facilitatorNotes: The old elves have long beards and wrinkled faces, yet work alongside youngsters with the same eagerness.
evidence: Along with youngsters did their best

questions.prompt: Why is buckling the harness not the end of their work?
facilitatorNotes: They still have to guide the shafts, balance the cart and back Mag into position. Invite the child to order these tasks in words.
evidence: The hardest task was yet to do.
In backing Mag into the cart.

days.title: The Brownies' Good Work — A harvest needing help (excerpt)
days.challenge: Connect descriptions of neglected crops to the farmer’s absence.
days.focus: Imagined voices from vegetables make a human problem urgent.
days.context: Brownies are imaginary little sprites who act secretly at night. A farmer has been hurt while stopping runaway horses to save children. This opening ends with the Brownies deciding that too little night remains to start work immediately. A picayune is a small coin.

excerpt.locator: THE BROWNIES' GOOD WORK. Text blocks 1–4; opening “ONE time, while Brownies passed around”; closing “Is left to set the matter right.”.

blocks.text:
ONE time, while Brownies passed around
An honest farmer's piece of ground,
They paused to view the garden fair
And fields of grain that needed care.
"My friends," said one who often spoke
About the ways of human folk,

"Now here's a case in point, I claim,
Where neighbors scarce deserve the name:
This farmer on his back is laid
With broken ribs and shoulder-blade,
Received, I hear, some weeks ago;
While at the village here below,
He checked a running team, to save
Some children from an early grave.
Now overripe his harvest stands
In waiting for the reaper's hands;
The piece of wheat we lately passed
Is shelling out at every blast.

Those pumpkins in that corner plot
Begin to show the signs of rot;
The mold has fastened on their skin,
The ripest ones are caving in,
And soon the pig in yonder sty
With scornful grunt would pass them by.
His Early Rose potatoes there
Are much in need of light and air;
The turnip withers where it lies,
The beet and carrot want to rise.
'Oh, pull us up!' they seem to cry
To every one that passes by;
'The frost will finish our repose,
The grubs are working at our toes;

Unless you come and save us soon,
We'll not be worth a picayune!'
The corn is breaking from the stalk,
The hens around the hill can walk,
And with their ever ready bill
May pick the kernels at their will.
His neighbors are a sordid crowd,
Who've such a shameful waste allowed
So wrapped in self some men can be,
Beyond their purse they seldom see;
'T is left for us to play the friend
And here a helping hand extend.
But as the wakeful chanticleer
Is crowing in the stable near,
Too little of the present night
Is left to set the matter right.

questions.prompt: Why is the farmer unable to bring in his harvest? How does that affect our view of him?
facilitatorNotes: He was badly hurt rescuing children, so the unharvested field is not evidence that he does not care.
evidence: He checked a running team, to save

questions.prompt: If the carrots and beets could speak, what help would they ask for? Why soon?
facilitatorNotes: Their imagined request is to be pulled up before frost and grubs ruin them.
evidence: 'Oh, pull us up!' they seem to cry

questions.prompt: Why is the complaint about the neighbours stronger than simply saying they are busy?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker says they notice only their own money and fail to help someone injured. Discuss this as the Brownie’s judgment, supported by the neglected harvest, not an independently proven account of every neighbour.
evidence: Beyond their purse they seldom see;

days.title: The Poultry and the Borough
days.challenge: Follow a hungry pair through meeting, planning, and splitting up.
days.focus: Animal appetites give familiar place names a playful second meaning.
days.context: Reynard is a traditional name for a fox. Poultry means domestic birds such as chickens; a borough is a district and sounds like “burrow,” an animal’s underground home. These are also London place names. The rhyme mentions hunting for food but depicts no capture.

excerpt.locator: The Poultry and the Borough; complete poem, opening “The Fox ran to London”, closing “And the Weasel in the Borough.”.

blocks.text:
The Fox ran to London
Starving for his dinner;
There he met the Weasel
Looking even thinner.

The Weasel said to Reynard,
"What shall be our pickin's?"
Said Reynard to the Weasel,
"Rabbits and Spring Chickens."

Then they went a-hunting,
And they did it very thorough,
The Fox in the Poultry
And the Weasel in the Borough.

questions.prompt: Why are the Fox and Weasel interested in finding food together?
facilitatorNotes: Both appear hungry: the Fox is starving and the Weasel looks thinner still. These details prepare their food conversation.
evidence: Starving for his dinner;
Looking even thinner.

questions.prompt: What two foods do they name before they hunt?
facilitatorNotes: Rabbits and spring chickens. Connect that plan to the final destinations, while treating the place-name connection as a joke rather than proof that they catch anything.
evidence: "Rabbits and Spring Chickens."

questions.prompt: Does the ending tell us that they caught their dinner? What does it actually show?
facilitatorNotes: It shows the Fox hunting in the Poultry and the Weasel in the Borough, but names no captured animal. A prediction may be discussed as a prediction, not an event in the text.
evidence:
The Fox in the Poultry
And the Weasel in the Borough.

days.title: The Boy and the Brook
days.challenge: Test the same request against three different replies.
days.focus: The boy wants to hold onto pleasures that depend on movement or change.
days.context: Read the boy’s requests in one voice and the brook, wind, and day in another.
days.contentNote: The wind calls stopping “death” in a figurative reply; no person dies.

excerpt.locator:
The Boy and the Brook; source blocks 447–449, beginning “Said the boy to the brook that was rippling away,
"Oh, little brook, pretty brook, will yo” and ending “the jewel of day would no longer seem bright,
If it were not clasped round by the setting of night."”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 107.

blocks.text:
Said the boy to the brook that was rippling away,
"Oh, little brook, pretty brook, will you not stay?
Oh, stay with me, play with me, all the day long,
And sing in my ears your sweet murmuring song."
Said the brook to the boy as it hurried away,
"And is't for my music you ask me to stay?
I was silent until from the hillside I gushed;
Should I pause for an instant, my song would be hushed."

Said the boy to the wind that was fluttering past,
"Oh, little wind, pretty wind, whither so fast?
Oh, stay with me, play with me, fan my hot brow,
And ever breathe softly and gently as now."
Said the wind to the boy as it hurried away,
"And is't for my coolness you ask me to stay?
'Tis only in flying you feel my cool breath;
Should I pause for an instant, that instant were death."

Said the boy to the day that was hurrying by,
"Oh, little day, pretty day, why must you fly?
Oh, stay with me, play with me, just as you are;
Let no shadow of evening your noon-brightness mar."
Said the day to the boy as it hurried away,
"And is't for my brightness you ask me to stay?
Know, the jewel of day would no longer seem bright,
If it were not clasped round by the setting of night."

questions.prompt: Why would stopping the brook spoil what the boy enjoys?
facilitatorNotes: Its moving water makes the sound he wants to keep; still water would not murmur in the same way.
evidence: Should I pause for an instant, my song would be hushed.

questions.prompt: How does the wind’s answer resemble the brook’s?
facilitatorNotes: Both say their movement creates the quality the boy loves. Stopping would remove that quality.
evidence: 'Tis only in flying you feel my cool breath;

questions.prompt: Does night actually clasp day like a jewel setting? What does that picture suggest?
facilitatorNotes: The comparison says brightness is noticed through contrast with darkness. It is a different explanation from the physical movement of wind and water.
evidence: the jewel of day would no longer seem bright,

days.title: Bluebird — a bird portrait (excerpt)
days.challenge: Connect changes in young birds with changes in a whole flock later in the year.
days.focus: Colour and movement give the season a visible ending.
days.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897. This middle-to-late passage follows discussion of bluebird nesting. Undulating means moving in a wave-like path.

excerpt.locator: Bluebird entry, narrative paragraphs beginning “When the young birds first emerge from the shell they are almost black; they come into the” and ending “to summer" when the bluebirds withdraw their touch of brightness from the dreary November landscape.”.

blocks.text: When the young birds first emerge from the shell they are almost black; they come into their splendid heritage of color by degrees, lest their young heads might be turned. It is only as they spread their tiny wings for their first flight from the nest that we can see a few blue feathers.

With the first cool days of autumn the bluebirds collect in flocks, often associating with orioles and kingbirds in sheltered, sunny places where insects are still plentiful. Their steady, undulating flight now becomes erratic as they take food on the wing—a habit that they may have learned by association with the kingbirds, for they have also adopted the habit of perching upon some conspicuous lookout and then suddenly launching out into the air for a passing fly and returning to their perch. Long after their associates have gone southward, they linger like the last leaves on the tree. It is indeed "good-bye to summer" when the bluebirds withdraw their touch of brightness from the dreary November landscape.

questions.prompt: Do newly hatched bluebirds immediately look as blue as their name suggests?
facilitatorNotes: No: they are nearly black, and only some blue feathers show at their first flight. The name describes an appearance they grow into.
evidence: When the young birds first emerge from the shell they are almost black;

questions.prompt: What new way of catching food does the author describe in autumn?
facilitatorNotes: The birds fly out from a perch for an insect and return, and also catch food on the wing. She suggests association with kingbirds as a possible explanation, not a certainty.
evidence: a habit that they may have learned by association with the kingbirds

questions.prompt: Why compare the remaining bluebirds to the last leaves on a tree?
facilitatorNotes: Both linger after others have gone and mark the late season; their final departure makes the landscape feel less bright.
evidence: they linger like the last leaves on the tree.

days.title: White-breasted Nuthatch — a bird portrait (excerpt)
days.challenge: Follow an upside-down animal through a description with several actions.
days.focus: The observer becomes an object of curiosity for the bird.
days.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897. Opera-glasses are small binoculars; the mercury going down means the temperature is falling. This passage follows a poem quoted in the book, which is outside the excerpt.

excerpt.locator: White-breasted Nuthatch entry, narrative paragraphs beginning “With more artless inquisitiveness than fear, this lively little acrobat stops his hammerin” and ending “ss, and often depositing as many as ten white eggs (speckled with red and lilac) for a single brood.”.

blocks.text: With more artless inquisitiveness than fear, this lively little acrobat stops his hammering or hatcheting at your approach, and stretching himself out from the tree until it would seem he must fall off, he peers down at you, head downward, straight into your upturned opera-glasses. If there is too much snow on the upper side of a branch, watch how he runs along underneath it like a fly, busily tapping the bark, or adroitly breaking the decayed bits with his bill, as he searches for the spider's eggs, larvæ, etc., hidden there; yet somehow, between mouthfuls, managing to call out his cheery quank! quank! hank! hank!

Titmice and nuthatches, which have many similar characteristics, are often seen in the most friendly hunting parties on the same tree. A pine woods is their dearest delight. There, as the mercury goes down, their spirits only seem to go up higher. In the spring they have been thought by many to migrate in flocks, whereas they are only retreating with their relations away from the haunts of men to the deep, cool woods, where they nest. With infinite patience the nuthatch excavates a hole in a tree, lining it with feathers and moss, and often depositing as many as ten white eggs (speckled with red and lilac) for a single brood.

questions.prompt: Who is inspecting whom when the nuthatch stops working?
facilitatorNotes: The person watches through glasses, but the bird stretches out and looks back down. The reversed inspection gives the encounter a lively, mutual quality.
evidence: he peers down at you, head downward, straight into your upturned opera-glasses.

questions.prompt: How does the bird keep searching when snow covers the top of a branch?
facilitatorNotes: It runs underneath, compared with a fly, and searches bark for food. Let the child trace the top and bottom of an imagined branch.
evidence: watch how he runs along underneath it like a fly

questions.prompt: What might look like migration but is explained differently here?
facilitatorNotes: The birds leave places near people for deep woods where they nest. The author distinguishes disappearing from our view from leaving the region.
evidence: they are only retreating with their relations away from the haunts of men

days.title: Red-breasted Nuthatch — a bird portrait (excerpt)
days.challenge: Use both appearance and sound to distinguish two related birds.
days.focus: A mixed winter flock becomes an imagined family party.
days.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897. The previous entry concerned the white-breasted nuthatch. Congener means a closely related animal, and Free masons here supplies a playful image of skilled workers.

excerpt.locator: Red-breasted Nuthatch entry, narrative paragraphs beginning “The brighter coloring of this tiny, hardy bird distinguishes it from the other and larger ” and ending “umn visitor, but latterly it is credited with habits like its congener's in nearly every particular.”.

blocks.text: The brighter coloring of this tiny, hardy bird distinguishes it from the other and larger nuthatch, with whom it is usually seen, for the winter birds have a delightfully social manner, so that a colony of these Free masons is apt to contain not only both kinds of nuthatches and chickadees, but kinglets and brown creepers as well. It shares the family habit of walking about the trees, head downward, and running along the under side of limbs like a fly. By Thanksgiving Day the quank! quank! of the white-breasted species is answered by the tai-tai-tait! of the red-breasted cousin in the orchard, where the family party is celebrating with an elaborate menu of slugs, insects' eggs, and oily seeds from the evergreen trees.

For many years this nuthatch, a more northern species than the white-breasted bird, was thought to be only a spring and autumn visitor, but latterly it is credited with habits like its congener's in nearly every particular.

questions.prompt: What helps distinguish this nuthatch from its larger relative besides size?
facilitatorNotes: Its brighter colouring and different call are clues. Encourage listening to tai-tai-tait and quank aloud as two different patterns.
evidence: The brighter coloring of this tiny, hardy bird distinguishes it

questions.prompt: Why is the “elaborate menu” a funny way to describe their Thanksgiving gathering?
facilitatorNotes: It gives a human holiday meal to birds, whose menu consists of slugs, eggs and seeds. The joke depends on the actual bird foods.
evidence: an elaborate menu of slugs, insects' eggs, and oily seeds

questions.prompt: Does the author present people’s earlier belief about when this bird visits as final?
facilitatorNotes: No: she contrasts a long-held belief with a later understanding closer to its relative’s habits. This is an example of an account changing with observation.
evidence: For many years this nuthatch, a more northern species than the white-breasted bird, was thought to be only a spring and autumn visitor

days.title: The Stock Exchange
days.challenge: Distinguish an imaginary flower trade from the businesslike words in its title.
days.focus: Place-name wordplay turns serious trading into a garden game.
days.context: Stocks are garden flowers. A bull and a bear are animals here, though those words also appear in talk about financial markets. No knowledge of money markets is needed to follow the flower swap.

excerpt.locator: The Stock Exchange; complete poem, opening “There's a Bull and a Bear, and what do you think?”, closing “They are always so busy exchanging their Stocks.”.

blocks.text:
There's a Bull and a Bear, and what do you think?
They live in a Garden of white Stocks and pink.
"I'll give you a pink Stock for one of your white,"
Says the Bear to the Bull; and the Bull says, "All right!"
They never make answer if anyone knocks,
They are always so busy exchanging their Stocks.

questions.prompt: What does the Bear offer, and what does he want in return?
facilitatorNotes: He offers a pink stock flower for a white one. Have the child retell both sides of the exchange rather than calling it simply buying.
evidence: "I'll give you a pink Stock for one of your white,"

questions.prompt: What tells us that the Bull agrees to the trade?
facilitatorNotes: His direct reply, “All right!”, accepts the offered exchange. The dialogue lets us hear agreement rather than having a narrator merely report it.
evidence: Says the Bear to the Bull; and the Bull says, "All right!"

questions.prompt: Why might someone knocking at the garden get no answer? What makes that amusing?
facilitatorNotes: The animals are so absorbed in repeatedly exchanging flowers that they ignore visitors. Children may hear a gentle joke about being extremely busy with a small task.
evidence: They are always so busy exchanging their Stocks.

days.title: A Howl about an Owl
days.challenge: Enjoy sound and deliberate absurdity without expecting realistic animal behavior.
days.focus: An elaborate courtship ends in a ridiculous mistake.
days.context: “Camlet” is a kind of cloth; the Lancers and the Chorus Jig are dances. This owl belongs to nonsense, not a bird guide.

excerpt.locator:
A Howl about an Owl; source blocks 573–577, beginning “It was an owl lived in an oak,
Sing heigh ho! the prowly owl!
He often smiled, but he seld” and ending “d wasn't that a sad disappointment for he!
Sing heigh ho! the howly fowl!
Tu-whit! tu-whit! tu-whoo!”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 139, 140.

blocks.text:
It was an owl lived in an oak,
Sing heigh ho! the prowly owl!
He often smiled, but he seldom spoke,
And he wore a wig and a camlet cloak.
Sing heigh ho! the howly fowl!
Tu-whit! tu-whit! tu-whoo!

He fell in love with the chickadee,
Sing heigh ho! the prowly owl!
He askèd her, would she marry he,
And they'd go and live in Crim Tartaree.
Sing heigh ho! the howly fowl!
Tu-whit! tu-whit! tu-whoo!

"'Tis true," says he, "you are far from big."
Sing heigh ho! the prowly owl!
"But you'll look twice as well when I've bought you a wig,
And I'll teach you the Lancers and the Chorus Jig."
Sing heigh ho! the howly fowl!
Tu-whit! tu-whit! tu-whoo!

"I'll feed you with honey when the moon grows pale."
Sing heigh ho! the prowly owl!
"I'll hum you a hymn, and I'll sing you a scale,
Till you quiver with delight to the tip of your tail!"
Sing heigh ho! the howly fowl!
Tu-whit! tu-whit! tu-whoo!

So he went for to marry of the chickadee,
Sing heigh ho! the prowly owl!
But the sun was so bright that he could not see,
So he marrièd the hoppergrass instead of she.
And wasn't that a sad disappointment for he!
Sing heigh ho! the howly fowl!
Tu-whit! tu-whit! tu-whoo!

questions.prompt: What does the owl promise to buy the chickadee, and why is it funny?
facilitatorNotes: A wig belongs to human dress; the owl thinks a small bird will look better with one, like his own.
evidence: when I've bought you a wig,

questions.prompt: Which repeated sounds let a listener join the poem?
facilitatorNotes: The howly/prowly rhymes and tu-whit/tu-whoo refrain imitate and exaggerate an owl’s call.
evidence: Tu-whit! tu-whit! tu-whoo!

questions.prompt: How does the last verse undo all the owl’s careful promises?
facilitatorNotes: He marries the wrong creature, a grasshopper, because he cannot see. The carefully planned future collapses into nonsense.
evidence: So he marrièd the hoppergrass instead of she.

days.title: Bobolink — a bird portrait (excerpt)
days.challenge: Follow seasonal changes in both appearance and sound.
days.focus: Family life connects a quieter song with a changing coat.
days.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897. The preceding part of the entry describes the male bobolink’s lively spring song. A moult is the shedding and replacement of feathers; insectivorous means eating insects.

excerpt.locator: Bobolink entry, narrative paragraphs beginning “After midsummer the cares of the family have so worn upon the jollity of our dashing, roll” and ending “insectivorous: grasshoppers, crickets, beetles, spiders, with seeds of grass especially for variety.”.

blocks.text: After midsummer the cares of the family have so worn upon the jollity of our dashing, rollicking friend that his song is seldom heard. The colors of his coat fade into a dull yellowish brown like that of his faithful mate, who has borne the greater burden of the season, for he has two complete moults each year.

The bobolinks build their nest on the ground in high grass. The eggs are of a bluish white. Their food is largely insectivorous: grasshoppers, crickets, beetles, spiders, with seeds of grass especially for variety.

questions.prompt: Which two changes would make a late-summer bobolink seem unlike the lively spring singer?
facilitatorNotes: His song becomes rare and his plumage turns dull yellowish brown. Invite the child to connect a sound change with a visible one.
evidence: his song is seldom heard.

questions.prompt: How does the author make the bird sound like a busy human parent?
facilitatorNotes: She speaks of family cares wearing down his jollity. Explain that this is a way of imagining the bird’s life, while the seasonal changes are the described observations.
evidence: the cares of the family have so worn upon the jollity

questions.prompt: Would looking high in tree branches be the best way to find the nest described here? Why?
facilitatorNotes: No: it is on the ground in tall grass. The setting differs from many familiar tree nests.
evidence: The bobolinks build their nest on the ground in high grass.

days.title: The Brownies And The Bees — Remembering the lost swarm (excerpt)
days.challenge: Distinguish an immediate guess from a memory offered as evidence.
days.focus: A discovery leads to a helping plan and then a caution.
days.context: Brownies are imaginary little sprites who act secretly at night. The Brownies hear bees in a tree. The passage ends before they act. Beekeeping language and animal behaviour reflect an old fantasy poem, not instructions for approaching bees.

excerpt.locator: THE BROWNIES AND THE BEES. Text blocks 1–4; opening “WHILE Brownies once were rambling through”; closing “To treat the buzzer with respect."”.

blocks.text:
WHILE Brownies once were rambling through
A forest where tall timber grew,
The hum of bees above their head
To much remark and wonder led.
They gazed at branches in the air
And listened at the roots with care,
And soon a pine of giant size
Was found to hold the hidden prize.
Said one: "Some wild bees here have made
Their home within the forest shade,
Where neither fox nor prying bear
Can steal the treasure gathered there."
Another spoke: "You're quick and bright,
And as a rule judge matters right;
But here, my friend, you're all astray,
And like the blind mole grope your way.
I chance well to remember still,
How months ago, when up the hill,
A farmer near, with bell and horn,
Pursued a swarm one sunny morn.
The fearful din the town awoke,
The clapper from his bell he broke;
But still their queen's directing cry

The bees heard o'er the clamor high;
And held their bearing for this pine
As straight as runs the county line.
With taxes here, and failures there,
The man can ill such losses bear.
In view of this, our duty's clear:
To-morrow night we'll muster here,
And when we give this tree a fall,
In proper shape we'll hive them all,
And take the queen and working throng
And lazy drones where they belong."

Next evening, at the time they'd set,
Around the pine the Brownies met
With tools collected, as they sped
From mill and shop and farmer's shed;
While some, to all their wants alive,
With ready hands procured a hive.

Ere work began, said one: "I fear
But little sport awaits us here.
Be sure a trying task we'll find;
The bee is fuss and fire combined.
Let's take him in his drowsy hour,
Or when palavering to the flower.
For bees, however wild or tame,
In all lands are about the same;
And those will rue it who neglect
To treat the buzzer with respect."

questions.prompt: Why does the second speaker doubt that these are wild bees?
facilitatorNotes: He remembers a farmer following a lost swarm toward this very pine. That observation is a reason to question the first guess.
evidence: Pursued a swarm one sunny morn.

questions.prompt: What reason beyond wanting honey do they give for returning the bees?
facilitatorNotes: The farmer has financial troubles and cannot afford the loss; they want to help him.
evidence: The man can ill such losses bear.

questions.prompt: How does “fuss and fire combined” change the mood of the plan?
facilitatorNotes: The image makes the bees seem noisy, active and potentially painful. It tempers the earlier confidence with respect and caution.
evidence: The bee is fuss and fire combined.

days.title: The Brownies Canoeing — A trip that stops being fun (excerpt)
days.challenge: Recognize that a promising beginning does not predict the whole trip.
days.focus: Changing river conditions reveal the difference between drifting and steering.
days.context: Brownies are imaginary little sprites who act secretly at night. The Brownies have launched borrowed canoes. This passage follows their river trip to its end; the narrator’s claim about every river is poetic exaggeration, not a geography rule.

excerpt.locator: THE BROWNIES CANOEING. Text blocks 6–12; opening “The start was promising and fine;”; closing “They soon were lost to sight and sound.”.

blocks.text:
The start was promising and fine;
With little skill and less design
They steered along as suited best,
And let the current do the rest.

All nature seemed to be aware
That something strange was stirring there.
The owl to-whooed, the raven croaked;
The mink and rat with caution poked
Their heads above the wave, aghast;
While frogs a look of wonder cast
And held their breath till all had passed.
As every stream will show a bend,
If one explores from end to end,

So every river, great and small,
Must have its rapids and its fall;
And those who on its surface glide
O'er rough as well as smooth must ride.
The stream whereon had started out
The Brownie band in gleeful rout

Was wild enough to please a trout.
At times it tumbled on its way
O'er shelving rocks and bowlders gray
At times it formed from side to side
A brood of whirlpools deep and wide
That with each other seemed to vie
As fated objects drifted nigh.
Ere long each watchful Brownie there,
Of all these facts grew well aware;
Some losing faith, as people will,
In their companions' care or skill,
Would seize the paddle for a time,

Until a disapproving chime
Of voices made them rest their hand,
And let still others take command.
But, spite of current, whirl or go,
In spite of hungry tribes below,--

The eel, the craw-fish, leech, and pout,
That watched them from the starting out,
And thought each moment flitting by
Might spill them out a year's supply,--
The Brownies drifted onward still;
And though confusion baffled skill,
Canoes throughout the trying race
Kept right side up in every case.
But sport that traveled hand in hand
With horrors hardly pleased the band,
As pallid cheek and popping eye
On every side could testify;
And all agreed that wisdom lay
In steering home without delay.

So landing quick, the boats they tied
To roots or trees as chance supplied,
And plunging in the woods profound,
They soon were lost to sight and sound.

questions.prompt: Why can they move successfully at first despite having little skill?
facilitatorNotes: The current carries them. That early ease hides the difficulty of controlling a canoe in rougher water.
evidence: And let the current do the rest.

questions.prompt: Does taking turns grabbing the paddle solve their problem? What does the poem show?
facilitatorNotes: Voices object and still others take command; confusion continues. The boats stay upright, but that lucky result does not mean the steering works well.
evidence: And though confusion baffled skill,

questions.prompt: What tells us that the Brownies themselves no longer regard the trip as enjoyable?
facilitatorNotes: Pale cheeks and staring eyes show fear, and they agree to head home. Their decision follows the experience rather than their first excitement.
evidence:
And all agreed that wisdom lay
In steering home without delay.

days.title: Wormwood Scrubbs
days.challenge: Track a cleaning list as it grows from household objects to an entire city.
days.focus: Exaggeration and repeated scrubbing make an impossible job sound energetic.
days.context: Wormwood Scrubs is a London place name. The poem invents a cleaner called Wormwood. “Elbow-grease” means hard physical effort, not a substance in a bottle; Saint Paul’s is a large cathedral.

excerpt.locator: Wormwood Scrubbs; complete poem, opening “Wormwood scrubs, Wormwood scrubs”, closing “She'll never get it clean!”.

blocks.text:
Wormwood scrubs, Wormwood scrubs
Windows, walls, and floors,
Pots and pans and pickle-tubs,
Tables, chairs and doors;
Wormwood scrubs the public seats
And the City Halls;
Wormwood scrubs the London streets,
Wormwood scrubs Saint Paul's;
Wormwood scrubs on her hands and knees,
But oh, it's plainly seen,
Though she use a ton of elbow-grease
She'll never get it clean!

questions.prompt: How does the cleaning job grow larger as the poem goes on?
facilitatorNotes: It starts with household surfaces and containers, then expands to public seats, city halls, streets, and Saint Paul’s. Ask the child to contrast one small object with one large place.
evidence: Pots and pans and pickle-tubs,
Wormwood scrubs the London streets,

questions.prompt: What do the repeated words “Wormwood scrubs” make you imagine about her movement?
facilitatorNotes: The repetition can sound like repeated back-and-forth strokes or endless work. Accept an alternative rhythm-based description tied to the recurring action.
evidence: Wormwood scrubs, Wormwood scrubs

questions.prompt: Does the poem think working even harder will finish the job? How can you tell?
facilitatorNotes: No: even a ton of effort will never get it clean. The enormous task and emphatic ending suggest impossibility, not laziness.
evidence: Though she use a ton of elbow-grease
She'll never get it clean!

days.title: Hopsy Upsy
days.challenge: Follow a practical sequence through extravagant images.
days.focus: An ordinary bath becomes a sparkling imagined landscape.
days.context: This is a grown-up’s song to a baby during washing and dressing.

excerpt.locator:
Hopsy Upsy; source blocks 475–480, beginning “Hopsy upsy, Baby oh!
Into your bath you now must go;
Splash and dash, and paddle and plash” and ending “ as silver they fall and flow.
Now toss him up and carry him down,
The bonniest Baby in Boston town!”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 114.

blocks.text:
Hopsy upsy, Baby oh!
Into your bath you now must go;
Splash and dash, and paddle and plash,
That's what you like, my Baby oh!

Where is the sponge for Baby oh?
See the silvery fountains flow,—
Diamond drops so bright and clear,
Falling all over my Baby dear.

Now for the soap, my Baby oh!
Watch the bubbles that come and go;
Rainbow isles in a sea of foam,
Reflecting your smiles, they go and come.

Here is the towel for Baby oh!
Cannot stay in all day, you know;
Now scrub and rub, and rub and scrub,
And so good-by to the beautiful tub.

Now for the shirt, my Baby oh!
Soft and warm, and as white as snow.
Puffy white petticoats, fluffy white gown;
Why, what a great ball of thistle-down!

Last come the curls, my Baby oh!
Soft as silver they fall and flow.
Now toss him up and carry him down,
The bonniest Baby in Boston town!

questions.prompt: Which object signals that the bath is ending?
facilitatorNotes: The towel follows soap and bubbles, then clothes and curls finish the routine.
evidence: Here is the towel for Baby oh!

questions.prompt: What are the “Rainbow isles” really?
facilitatorNotes: Soap bubbles seem like little rainbow islands floating in foam. Ask what colors and shapes make the image work.
evidence: Rainbow isles in a sea of foam,

questions.prompt: How do “scrub and rub, and rub and scrub” help someone perform the poem?
facilitatorNotes: The reversed repeated words create a back-and-forth rhythm that fits drying the baby.
evidence: Now scrub and rub, and rub and scrub,

days.title: Barn Swallow — a bird portrait (excerpt)
days.challenge: Notice how movement words do work that colour description cannot.
days.focus: A portrait admits the limits of words while vividly describing flight.
days.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897. The author is describing an American swallow and distinguishes it from a European relative. Gyrating means circling; a rafter is a beam supporting a roof.

excerpt.locator: Barn Swallow entry, narrative paragraphs beginning “Any one who attempts to describe the coloring of a bird's plumage knows how inadequate wor” and ending “usly spotted with brown and lilac that were all too familiar in the marauding days of our childhood.”.

blocks.text: Any one who attempts to describe the coloring of a bird's plumage knows how inadequate words are to convey a just idea of the delicacy, richness, and brilliancy of the living tints. But, happily, the beautiful barn swallow is too familiar to need description. Wheeling about our barns and houses, skimming over the fields, its bright sides flashing in the sunlight, playing "cross tag" with its friends at evening, when the insects, too, are on the wing, gyrating, darting, and gliding through the air, it is no more possible to adequately describe the exquisite grace of a swallow's flight than the glistening buff of its breast.

This is a typical bird of the air, as an oriole is of the trees and a sparrow of the ground. Though the swallow may often be seen perching on a telegraph wire, suddenly it darts off as if it had received a shock of electricity, and we see the bird in its true element.
While this swallow is peculiarly American, it is often confounded with its European cousin Hirundo rustica in noted ornithologies.

Up in the rafters of the barn, or in the arch of an old bridge that spans a stream, these swallows build their bracket-like nests of clay or mud pellets intermixed with straw. Here the noisy little broods pick their way out of the white eggs curiously spotted with brown and lilac that were all too familiar in the marauding days of our childhood.

questions.prompt: The author says the bird is hard to describe. Which movement words nevertheless help you see it?
facilitatorNotes: Wheeling, skimming, darting and gliding offer different motions. Invite the child to choose two and explain their difference rather than merely repeat a list.
evidence: gyrating, darting, and gliding through the air

questions.prompt: Why call the swallow a bird of the air even when it is sitting on a wire?
facilitatorNotes: The perch is temporary; sudden flight returns it to what the author calls its true element. The electrical-shock comparison makes the departure seem quick.
evidence: suddenly it darts off as if it had received a shock of electricity

questions.prompt: What combination of materials and location makes the nest different from a twig nest in a tree?
facilitatorNotes: Mud or clay mixed with straw forms a bracket-like structure under rafters or a bridge arch. Mention both construction and placement.
evidence: these swallows build their bracket-like nests of clay or mud pellets intermixed with straw.

days.title: The Brownies On Roller Skates — Watching the rink (excerpt)
days.challenge: Hear a character build a case by listing earlier adventures.
days.focus: A new desire grows from both sound and spectacle.
days.context: Brownies are imaginary little sprites who act secretly at night. The Brownies have reached town and are looking for the skating hall. They observe from its roof and plan to enter after people leave; the actual skating follows outside this excerpt.

excerpt.locator: THE BROWNIES ON ROLLER SKATES. Text blocks 6–11; opening “Now, guided by the rumbling sound”; closing “We may command when set on wheels."”.

blocks.text:
Now, guided by the rumbling sound
That told where skaters circled 'round,
Through dimly lighted streets they flew,
And close about the building drew.

Without delay the active band,
By spouts and other means at hand,
Of skill and daring furnished proof
And gained possession of the roof;
Then through the skylight viewed the show
Presented by the crowds below.

Said one: "While I survey that floor
I'm filled with longing more and more,

And discontent with me will bide
Till 'round the rink I smoothly glide.
At night I've ridden through the air,
Where bats abide, and owls repair;
I've rolled in surf of ocean wide,
And coasted down the mountain-side;
And now to sweep around a hall
On roller skates would crown it all."

"My plans," the leader answer made,
"Are in my mind already laid.
Within an hour the folk below
Will quit their sport and homeward go;

Then will the time be ripe, indeed,
For us to leave this roof with speed,
And prove how well our toes and heels
We may command when set on wheels."

questions.prompt: How do the Brownies find the skating hall before they can see its floor?
facilitatorNotes: They follow the rumbling sound through the streets. It is a useful sound clue rather than a map or sign.
evidence: Now, guided by the rumbling sound

questions.prompt: Why does one Brownie mention flying, ocean surf, and coasting?
facilitatorNotes: He lists other pleasures to show how much he still wants this new one; skating would “crown” his experiences.
evidence: On roller skates would crown it all.

questions.prompt: Why does the leader choose to wait an hour?
facilitatorNotes: He expects the humans to leave and the hall to become available for the secretive Brownies. The plan depends on timing.
evidence: Will quit their sport and homeward go;

days.title: The Brownies At Lawn-Tennis
days.challenge: Hear the difference between careful preparation and disorderly play.
days.focus: Tennis vocabulary makes the game sound orderly before the Brownies bend its rules.
days.context: Brownies are imaginary little sprites who act secretly at night. Tennis uses rackets, a net, marked courts, and special scoring calls such as deuce. Children need not master scoring to notice the contrast.

excerpt.locator: THE BROWNIES AT LAWN-TENNIS. Text blocks 1–5; opening “ONE evening as the woods grew dark,”; closing “And Brownies all must disappear.”.

blocks.text:
ONE evening as the woods grew dark,
The Brownies wandered through a park.
And soon a building, quaint and small,
Appeared to draw the gaze of all.
Said one: "This place contains, no doubt,
The tools of workmen hereabout."
Another said: "You're quite astray,
The workmen's tools are miles away;
Within this building may be found
The fixtures for the tennis ground.
A meadow near, both long and wide,
For half the year is set aside,
And marked with many a square and court,
For those who love the royal sport.
On afternoons assembled there,
The active men and maidens fair
Keep up the game until the day
Has faded into evening gray."
"In other lands than those we tread,
I played the game," another said,
"And proved my skill and muscle stout,
As 'server' and as 'striker-out.'
The lock that hangs before us there
Bears witness to the keeper's care,
And tramps or burglars might go by,
If such a sign should meet the eye.
But we, who laugh at locks or law
Designed to keep mankind in awe,
May praise the keeper's cautious mind,
But all the same an entrance find."

Ere long, the path that lay between
The building and the meadow green,
Was crowded with the bustling throng,
All bearing implements along;
Some lugging stakes or racket sets,
And others buried up in nets.
To set the posts and mark the ground
The proper size and shape around,
With service-line and line of base,
And courts, both left and right, in place,
Was work that caused but slight delay;
And soon the sport was under way.
And then a strange and stirring scene
Was pictured out upon the green.

Some watched the game and noted well
Where this or that one would excel.

And shouts and calls that filled the air
Proved even-handed playing there.
With anxious looks some kept the score,
And shouted "'vantage!" "game all!" or
To some, "love, forty!"--"deuce!" to more.
But when "deuce set!" the scorer cried,
Applause would ring on every side.
At times so hot the contest grew,
Established laws aside they threw,
And in the game where four should stand,
At least a dozen took a hand.
Some tangled in the netting lay
And some from base-lines strayed away.
Some hit the ball when out of place
Or scrambled through unlawful space.
But still no game was forced to halt
Because of this or greater fault.

And there they sported on the lawn
Until the ruddy streaks of dawn
Gave warning that the day was near,
And Brownies all must disappear.

questions.prompt: What corrects the first guess about what is stored in the little building?
facilitatorNotes: Another Brownie identifies tennis equipment and describes the nearby court and its daytime players.
evidence: The fixtures for the tennis ground.

questions.prompt: Which preparations show that they know a court needs more than a ball and rackets?
facilitatorNotes: They set posts and mark service lines, baselines and courts. Invite two details rather than a full equipment list.
evidence: With service-line and line of base,

questions.prompt: How does the number of players turn an orderly game into a crowded joke?
facilitatorNotes: A dozen join where four should stand; tangles and wrong positions follow, but they keep playing.
evidence: And in the game where four should stand,
At least a dozen took a hand.

days.title: Saint John's Wood
days.challenge: Compare the leafy place described first with the changed place at the end.
days.focus: Green-to-grey contrast makes a playful place-name poem feel wistful.
days.context: Saint John’s Wood is a London place name. Farjeon imagines a figure living among animals and trees; this is poetic invention, not a documented account of a saint’s life. A haunch is the upper part of an animal’s back leg.

excerpt.locator: Saint John's Wood; complete poem, opening “Saint John walked in a Wood”, closing “But where's the good Saint John?”.

blocks.text:
Saint John walked in a Wood
Where elm-trees spread their branches
And Squirrels climbed and Pigeons cooed.
And Hares sat on their haunches.
He built him willow huts
Wherever he might settle;
His meat was chiefly hazel-nuts,
His drink the honey-nettle.
His Wood that grew so green
Is now as grey as stone;
His Wood may any day be seen,
But where's the good Saint John?

questions.prompt: Which creatures make the first Wood seem alive? Choose two and say what they do.
facilitatorNotes: Squirrels climb, pigeons coo, and hares sit on their haunches. The different motions and sound fill the wood with life.
evidence: And Squirrels climbed and Pigeons cooed.
And Hares sat on their haunches.

questions.prompt: How do the willow huts and hazel-nuts connect Saint John to the Wood?
facilitatorNotes: He finds shelter and food in its plants. Invite the child to connect each detail to a need, rather than making unsupported claims about his whole life.
evidence: He built him willow huts
His meat was chiefly hazel-nuts,

questions.prompt: Why might the final question feel different from the cheerful opening?
facilitatorNotes: The Wood changes from green to grey, and the person is missing. Children may hear sadness, curiosity, or surprise; support the feeling with the change and question.
evidence:
His Wood that grew so green
Is now as grey as stone;
But where's the good Saint John?

days.title: The Fairies
days.challenge: Revise a first interpretation when a second speaker offers clues.
days.focus: A mother uses fairy language to reveal her delight in children.
days.context: The first five verses are the child’s questions. The next five are the mother’s reply; change voices at “True it is.”
days.contentNote: The closing blessing expresses the mother’s religious language.

excerpt.locator:
The Fairies; source blocks 203–212, beginning “Is it true, my mother?
Can it really be,
That the little fairies
Every day you see?
Oh! th” and ending “ook into the glass, dear!
One of them you'll see.
Oh! the little fairies,
God bless them all for me!”. Full selected text also collated against Roberts Brothers 1890, scan leaves 56, 57, 58, 59.

blocks.text:
Is it true, my mother?
Can it really be,
That the little fairies
Every day you see?
Oh! the little fairies,
Wonderful and wise,
Have you really seen them
With your own two eyes?

Tell me where their home is,
Dearest mother mine.
Is it in the garden
'Neath the clustering vine?
Is it in the meadow,
'Mid the grasses tall?
Is it by the brookside,
Sweetest place of all?

Deep within the woodland,
Shall I find them then,—
Pretty little maidens,
Pretty little men;
Curled among the roseleaves,
Stretched along the fern,
Where no wind can shake them,
And no sunbeams burn?

Does the little queen live
In a great red rose,
Twenty elves to fan her
When to sleep she goes;
Coverlet of lilies
Sprinkled o'er with pearls,
Golden stars a-twinkling
In her golden curls?

Do they paint the flowers?
Do they teach the birds
All their lovely music,
With its strange, sweet words?
Oh! but tell me, mother!
Is it really true?
And when next you seek them,
Will you take me too?

True it is, my darling,
True as true can be,
That the little fairies
Every day I see,
Not within the meadow,
Not in woodland gloom,
But in brightest sunshine,
In this very room.

Singing like the robin,
Chirping like the wren,
Pretty little maidens,
Pretty little men;
Leaning o'er my shoulder,
Swinging on my chair,
Oh! the little fairies,
I see them everywhere.

Peeping at the window,
Peeping at the door,
If I bid them scamper,
Peeping all the more.
Little sweetest voices
Laughing merrily,
Oh! the little fairies,
They'll never let me be.

Tugging at my apron,
Twitching at my gown,
Climbing up into my lap,
Rumble-tumbling down.
Naughty little blue eyes,
Full of impish glee,
Oh! the little fairies,
They'll never let me be!

All are kings and queens, dear,
Every smallest one;
And on mother's knee here
Is their regal throne.
Look into the glass, dear!
One of them you'll see.
Oh! the little fairies,
God bless them all for me!

questions.prompt: Where does the child imagine the fairies might live?
facilitatorNotes: Garden, meadow, brookside, woodland, and a rose palace are possibilities; the mother will redirect this search indoors.
evidence: Is it by the brookside,

questions.prompt: Which actions begin to reveal what the mother means by fairies?
facilitatorNotes: Peeping, tugging her apron, climbing into her lap, and tumbling down describe playful children.
evidence: Tugging at my apron,

questions.prompt: Why does the mother tell the child to look in the glass?
facilitatorNotes: A mirror will show the child as one of the “fairies.” This gives the riddle’s answer rather than showing a separate magical creature.
evidence: Look into the glass, dear!

days.title: Cedar Bird — a bird portrait (excerpt)
days.challenge: Separate observable actions from the human manners the writer imagines.
days.focus: Quiet flock behaviour becomes a portrait of elaborate politeness.
days.context: This is historical nature writing from a 1923 edition of a book first published in 1897. Cedar bird is a name used here for the cedar waxwing. Gregarious means living in groups; gormandized means eaten heartily. This excerpt begins with the flock’s quiet voices.

excerpt.locator: Cedar Bird entry, narrative paragraphs beginning “One listens in vain for a song; only a lisping "Twee-twee-ze," or "a dreary whisper," as M” and ending “e never guilty of jolting or crowding. Few birds care to take life so easily, not to say indolently.”.

blocks.text: One listens in vain for a song; only a lisping "Twee-twee-ze," or "a dreary whisper," as Minot calls their low-toned communications with each other, reaches our ears from their high perches in the cedar trees, where they sit, almost motionless hours at a time, digesting the enormous quantities of juniper and whortle berries, wild cherries, worms, and insects upon which they have gormandized.

Nuttall gives the cedar birds credit for excessive politeness to each other. He says he has often seen them passing a worm from one to another down a whole row of beaks and back again before it was finally eaten.

When nesting time arrives—that is to say, towards the end of the summer—they give up their gregarious habits and live in pairs, billing and kissing like turtle-doves in the orchard or wild crab-trees, where a flat, bulky nest is rather carelessly built of twigs, grasses, feathers, strings—any odds and ends that may be lying about. The eggs are usually four, white tinged with purple and spotted with black.

Apparently they have no moulting season; their plumage is always the same, beautifully neat and full-feathered. Nothing ever hurries or flusters them, their greatest concern apparently being, when they alight, to settle themselves comfortably between their over-polite friends, who are never guilty of jolting or crowding. Few birds care to take life so easily, not to say indolently.

questions.prompt: What would a listener hear instead of a full song?
facilitatorNotes: A low lisping or whispering call. The lack of loud song suits the description of birds resting high in trees after feeding.
evidence: only a lisping "Twee-twee-ze,"

questions.prompt: What actual action leads Nuttall to call the birds excessively polite?
facilitatorNotes: They pass a worm along a row and back before it is eaten. Discuss the observed passing separately from the imagined human motive of politeness.
evidence: passing a worm from one to another down a whole row of beaks and back again

questions.prompt: When does the flock stop behaving like one large social company?
facilitatorNotes: At nesting time it breaks into pairs. The author shifts from flock manners to the work and intimacy of nesting.
evidence: they give up their gregarious habits and live in pairs

days.title: The Brownies At The Seaside — At the water’s edge (excerpt)
days.challenge: Compare different swimmers’ choices and the group’s shared limit.
days.focus: Individual confidence varies within one joyful crowd.
days.context: Brownies are imaginary little sprites who act secretly at night. The Brownies have reached the beach and put on bathing clothes. This closing passage describes their swim and return plan. The activities belong to a fantasy, not a swimming lesson.

excerpt.locator: THE BROWNIES AT THE SEASIDE. Text blocks 11–15; opening “Then, when a boat was manned with care”; closing “To sport in rolling surf again.”.

blocks.text:
Then, when a boat was manned with care
To watch for daring swimmers there,--

Lest some should venture, over-bold,
And fall a prey to cramp and cold,--
A few began from piers to leap
And plunge at once in water deep,
But more to shiver, shrink, and shout
As step by step they ventured out;
While others were content to stay
In shallow surf, to duck and play
Along the lines that people laid
To give the weak and timid aid.

It was a sight one should behold,
When o'er the crowd the breakers rolled;--
One took a header through the wave,
One floated like a chip or stave,
While others there, at every plunge,
Were taking water like a sponge.

But while the surf they tumbled through,
They reckoned moments as they flew,
And kept in mind their homeward race
Before the sun should show his face.

For sad and painful is the fate
Of those who roam abroad too late;
And well may Brownies bear in mind
The hills and vales they leave behind,
When far from native haunts they run,
As oft they do, in quest of fun.
But, ere they turned to leave the strand,
They made a vow with lifted hand
That every year, when summer's glow
Had warmed the ocean spread below,
They'd journey far from grove and glen
To sport in rolling surf again.

facilitatorNotes: The boat watches for overbold swimmers who may suffer cramp or cold. It shows concern about trouble even in this playful scene.
evidence: To watch for daring swimmers there,--

questions.prompt: Do all the Brownies choose to leap into deep water?
facilitatorNotes: No: some creep in, and others stay in shallow surf holding aid lines. The scene contains different comfort levels.
evidence:
While others were content to stay
In shallow surf, to duck and play

questions.prompt: What two plans do they keep in mind while enjoying the waves?
facilitatorNotes: They must get home before sunrise, yet they also promise to return each warm summer. The immediate departure does not end their love of the beach.
